speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware, I have just returned from the International Conference on Viet Nam which I attended as the representative of the government of Canada. Essentially, this was a conference of the great powers and the belligerents in the Viet Nam war. Canada was present because of our participation in the International Commission for Control and Supervision.
As members will recall, I made clear prior to my departure that we were not going to Paris to sit in judgment on the political and military settlements embodied in the Paris agreement. I have made it clear repeatedly that Canada has not sought, and is not seeking, a truce supervisory role in Indochina but was prepared to serve in such a capacity if we were convinced that the ICCS could be made to play a useful and effective role in restoring peace in Viet Nam.
I have also made clear in this House and outside it the conditions we would consider essential if we are to continue our participation in the ICCS. One of these essential conditions was the establishment of an outside political authority independent of the belligerents themselves to which the commission could send its reports and which could alert the international community to a serious threat to the peace in Viet Nam. Provision for such a mechanism was lacking in the January 27 agreement and it was our hope that this deficiency would be corrected by this conference. I therefore went to Paris to do all I could to see if a satisfactory authority could be established.
In my initial intervention at the conference on February 26 I expressed our views on this subject clearly and forcefully and placed before the participants a proposal that provided for the Secretary General of the United Nations to receive and circulate communications from the International Commission of Control and Supervision to the membership of the international conference, and to perform a similar function regarding the comments of the membership of the conference on such communications. The Canadian proposal also contained a provision for the reconvening of the conference on any of four conditions:
(a)	on receipt of a request from the International Commission of Control and Supervision;
(b)	on receipt of a request from the Four-Party Joint Military Commission or the Two-Party Joint Military Commission;
(c)	on receipt of a formal request from five of the members of the conference, excluding the Secretary General of the United Nations; and
(d)	after determining, at the request of any member of the conference that a two-thirds majority of the members, excluding the Secretary General, considered that there was cause to reconvene the conference.
It soon became clear that few participants at the conference were prepared to support the type of independent international reporting mechanism, involving the Secretary General of the United Nations, such as we had suggested and some were strongly opposed to the whole concept. I think it is safe to say that it was only because of our insistence on this matter that the conference addressed itself at all seriously to the matter. What finally emerged in Articles 6 and 7 of the act was the most that could be obtained. Under these arrangements, the reports and views of the international commission will at least be transmitted outside the closed circuit of the belligerents to the conference participants, and the conference itself can be recalled.
I made clear to the conference our disappointment that it could not agree on a more effective arrangement and I questioned whether the mechanism established went far enough and whether it could work. I emphasized to the conference on March 1 that the arrangements provided in Articles 6 and 7 would be carefully reviewed by the Canadian government in determining the extent to which our conditions for continued participation in the conference had been fulfilled.
The act provided an opportunity for world powers to acknowledge their respect and support for the January 27 agreement in association not only with the parties to that agreement, but also with the governments participating in the International Commission established under it. It is also noteworthy that the conference was conducted in the presence of the Secretary General of the United Nations.
I signed the act on behalf of Canada because the spirit of the act and the good will reflected in it were such as to command the support of the Canadian people. The act welcomes peace in Viet Nam and it calls for the participants to do nothing to jeopardize that peace. It was, therefore, important to have all the participants at the conference associated with those objectives, and failure to sign could have been open to misinterpretation. Moreover, not to have signed the act could only have been construed as meaning that one of our sine qua non had not been met. We were not in a position at the conference, nor are we yet in a position, to say whether the machinery provided in
1866

International Conference on Viet Nam
Articles 6 and 7 could serve the purpose we have had in mind. We will look at these arrangements in the light of our experience in the International Commission. This will be one of the prime factors in determining whether the commission is playing or can play an effective role in restoring peace to Viet Nam.
We must now, Mr. Speaker, examine very carefully the political authority and the reporting arrangements that have been established to determine whether, in our judgment, they have a reasonable prospect of operating effectively. We must also relate these arrangements to the effectiveness of the International Commission on the ground. The Canadian delegation under the direction of Ambassador Gauvin is making a tremendous effort to see that the commission works. But we cannot do it alone, Mr. Speaker, and disturbing developments in Viet Nam compel us to question whether the International Commission will be allowed to function in a way that would justify our continued participation. Perhaps-and I cannot say that I am very confident-the discussions in Paris will result in increased support by all the participants at the conference for the objectives we have in mind. Over the next few weeks, therefore, we will need to assess the relevant factors very carefully. It may be, Mr. Speaker, that at some time I should pay a visit to Viet Nam and see the situation on the ground for myself. If so, I would invite members of the opposition to come with me, but that is a decision that has not yet definitely been made. I will report to cabinet on the results of this assessment and the government will then be in a position to make its decision.
Perhaps I should emphasize again that the peace in Viet Nam depends upon the parties to the peace agreement itself. The International Commission can help by investigation and observation and reporting but it cannot keep the peace. The commission is not an essential element. It can be of help only if the parties-and that means all of them-wish to see the commission function.
I wish to table, Mr. Speaker, the text of the act of the International Conference on Viet Nam and copies of my statements to the conference on February 26 and March 1. It might be useful, since they are really part of the statement I have made today, if they could be printed either as an appendix to Hansard or as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are pleased to welcome back the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). We wished him good luck when he left but, unfortunately, we notice that our wishes for his success did not materialize.

The minister has reported to the House his failure to secure acceptance of what he termed himself before his departure a sine qua non condition to our continuing participation in the International Control Commission. The conference's new position is virtually without meaning and constitutes a watered down and unacceptable version of the minister's proposal. This failure leaves the government with but one alternative. It has been summed up very clearly by many observers who have expressed themselves over the weekend. One Montreal paper expressed it this way:
A continuing Canada presence will not stand for devotion to duty but rather for bluff, backdown and bumbling.
Our view all along has been that the minister should not have involved Canada without prior consultation with parliament-

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext:
-and without prior acceptance by all parties involved of the essential conditions.
As a nation, we should not apologize for desiring structures that will ensure a peace that can be supervised. The minister not only implies apology but indicates that for all intents and purposes we have backed down.
If a middle power has any long term interest it is in peace arrangements that guarantee an effective role for neutral smaller powers. If we do not stand by our own ground rules now, we will not succeed in letting belligerents know that the ground rules exist and must exist in the future.
The minister has disregarded parliament, has left dormant on the order paper the resolution calling for a debate and vote, and now, in spite of the difficulties in which he finds himself, the minister continues on behalf of the government to show continued disregard of the role of this House. He stated with arrogance yesterday that parliament will not be consulted before a final decision is reached. On the part of a weak minority government, the behaviour of the minister cannot be condoned.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS

March 5, 1973

before the House prior to committing the government to action on this matter.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext:
As to the continuation of our contribution to the commission, we would deeply regret if the arrangements or machinery for ending the war and restoring peace in Viet Nam broke down. But it remains true, as we said in an earlier statement, that the observer team can perform no useful function if the parties do not themselves accept the ceasefire or do not accept the provisions of the agreement in any important respect. No outside observer team or peacekeeping arrangement can enforce an agreement which the two parties themselves do not accept in good faith.
So far the ceasefire has been only partial and the observer team has been frustrated in performing its supposed function by lack of an adequate international body to whom to report and lack of a proper and workable procedure for reporting. We share the doubts of the minister as to the effectiveness of clauses six and seven of the Paris Act. We, along with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, would much have preferred the Security Council or the Secretary General of the United Nations to have been designated as the international authority to which the observers would report.
If the present situation continues without improvement-and I say "if"-then Canada must not repeat the farce of the International Control Commission.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext:
But I repeat-and in this I differ from the views expressed by the spokesman for the Official Opposition-if the observer team can function effectively, and we have not made a judgment on this aspect, then we would support the government in continuing the Canadian contribution.
The picture is not all dark. The arrangement made last week for the further release of United States prisoners of war and the continued withdrawal of United States troops from Viet Nam are to be welcomed, as is the international endorsement of the peace agreement reached in Paris.
I should like once again to refer briefly to the question of the release of the 200,000 political prisoners in South Viet Nam as constituting an integral part of a peaceful settlement. Many of these prisoners are neutral or noncommunist politicians. Many are students, teachers or religious leaders. They constitute the third force which is so essential to the genuine national reconciliation that is the core of the peace agreement. One of the reasons I hope Canada may be able to continue its participation in the work of the commission is that it could use its membership as a measure of leverage in urging that this immense tragedy be relieved.
Lastly, a word on reconstruction. The international community must make it clear that international aid for reconstruction in Viet Nam is contingent upon a genuine peace and the bona fide acceptance of the peace agreement by all parties. The absence of any reference to these
International Conference on Viet Nam
issues in the minister's statement presumably means that they were not the subject of serious discussion at the international conference. This is much to be regretted. These questions must be solved if genuine peace is to come to Viet Nam.
We look forward to further frank and full exploration of the situation in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. Following that full study, we want our share of participation in reaching the decision on whether or not we should continue to participate.

subsubtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE ON VIET NAM HELD IN PARIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Viet Nam conference in Paris has shown us that bringing peace to Viet Nam is going to be a difficult and even a painful business. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was full of optimism when he went to the conference, but he no doubt discovered very quickly that, however good his intentions, his proposals would not gain immediate acceptance, because not just one but both sides were represented at the conference. And unlike here in the House, even though we do have a pretty strong opposition, there seem to have been greatly differing opinions.
I am by no means sure, Mr. Speaker, if the suggestion or proposal of the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have had much success even if it had been accepted and carried out.
It must be admitted that United Nations achievements so far in the field of worldwide peace-keeping have been somewhat inconclusive.
It may be that we have nothing better to propose when it comes to trying to reconcile countries in conflict, especially when they have been at war for almost 30 years; however, if the United Nations is to become an effective instrument in future situations of this kind, I believe it will need to undergo some reforms.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has now committed herself to continuing to seek a way of bringing peace to Viet Nam, and I think that we should continue the debate that we started at the beginning of this session, on a subject that is still on the Order Paper, to give Parliament an opportunity to express its opinion.
I recall that in a very similar situation in 1964, under rather complicated circumstances, the government saw fit to ask for the support of the House for sending troops for peace-keeping in Cyprus.
I have always wondered why the government did not do likewise when it came to sending troops to Viet Nam for observation duties after the cease-fire. At all events, Mr. Speaker, I and my colleagues in the opposition consider that Parliament ought to be consulted on any further steps that might be taken.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill C-155, to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE GOVERNMENTS AND AGENCIES THEREOF SUBJECT TO ACT
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO MAKE GOVERNMENTS AND AGENCIES THEREOF SUBJECT TO ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill adds a new clause to the Navigable Waters Protection Act to make Her Majesty in right of Canada, in right of the provinces, or agencies of Her Majesty, subject to the terms of the act. Many activities of the governments of Canada and the provinces and their agents now affect navigable waters in ways similar to non-governmental activities. It is therefore proper and necessary that the act clearly require that governmental activities are subject to the same conditions and approvals.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

subsubtopic: POST OFFICE-POLICY OF SELLING PRE-STAMPED COLOURED SCENIC POSTCARDS
speechtext:
1.	Has the Post Office Department commenced a policy of selling prestamped coloured scenic postcards and, if so (a) on what date was this policy begun (b) for what reason?
2.	Has the government received any protests over this invasion of private business?
3.	(a) What has the program cost to date (b) what have been the revenues to date?

subsubtopic: POST OFFICE-POLICY OF SELLING PRE-STAMPED COLOURED SCENIC POSTCARDS
speechtext:
1. Yes. (a) Prestamped picture postcards were introduced for sale in most regular post office locations beginning July 24, 1972. (b) Prestamped scenic postcards are offered as a convenience to post office customers and as an extension of the sale of prestamped stationery which the Canada Post Office has been engaged in for more than 100 years. A series of prestamped monochrome scenic postcards was offered for sale in 1930. Prestamped stationery displaces separate transactions for postage stamps and eliminates the need by the customer to handle, moisten and affix postage stamps.
2.	Yes, but we do not believe the sale of special prestamped postcards through post office outlets represents an invasion of the commercial market for postcards. The scenes illustrated on the prestamped postcards were selected in cooperation with Provincial officials who were enthusiastic about the opportunity to promote areas of their provinces not normally featured on commercial postcards. Commercial cards tend to depict popular tourist areas or specific points of interest, whereas the scenes on the prestamped postcards are representative of the provinces generally. The cards are sold through postal outlets only, and in packages containing five cards. Most post offices therefore are carrying only one package of

five cards for sale; that is to say, the five cards relating to the province in which the post office is located. The selling price is $1 per package. Excluding the stamp value, the price of an individual card would be 12c/, which is two cents higher than the prevailing price for commercially retailed postcards. The prestamped postcards are of special interest to the stamp collecting community and a representative group of stamp collectors has endorsed the philatelic aspects of the sale of these cards. Since there is a significant number of collectors of Canadian stamps and postal stationery located outside Canada, the prestamped cards help to advertise the beauty of Canada to collectors in other countries. The primary objective of the sale of the prestamped scenic postcards is customer convenience and reduced stamp sales transactions and with this in mind the Canada Post Office is prepared to discuss the possibility of private postcard manufacturers producing prestamped picture postcards for distribution and sale through commercial retail channels.
3.	(a) $228,643. (b) $258,624. A major part of the costs stated in (a) was made up of initial manufacturing and advertising costs which will not be repeated to the same extent. speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: SHARE OF REVENUE FROM PERSONAL INCOME TAX TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Under the British North America Act, each provincial government has exclusive jurisdiction over the municipal institutions in its province. It is the responsibility of the provincial government to determine the allocation of responsibilities between itself and its municipalities, and to decide how much taxing authority should be delegated to the municipal institutions. Thus the federal government cannot give city councils a share of the revenue from personal income taxes. Through a variety of measures over the past 20 years, the federal government has reduced its share of the total personal income tax and provinces have increased their share. Increased provincial revenues from personal income taxes, as well as other taxes and revenues, have been accompanied by increased provincial transfers to their municipalities.

activities of the unemployment insurance benefit control operation in this area under discussion is a pre-selection in certain areas of claimants whose occupations fit job vacancies that have also been identified through manpower in those areas. First, we say that the income tax form is, in fact, confusing. Second, we say it is illegal in certain respects. Third, we suggest that the government should be giving financial aid to those individuals in our country who must now attempt to cope with the form. Fourth, because of the complexity of the form, we say that an extension of time should be offered to these harassed taxpayers to allow them to effectively deal with their own individual tax position. Fifth, we suggest that the government should expedite the payment of tax refunds, which may be some $1 billion in aggregate, to the six million taxpayers who will be receiving such refunds. Finally, we believe the time has long past when this government should have legalized the 1972 tax structure and the forms with respect to that tax structure.
Before dealing in detail with the points that I have enumerated, Mr. Speaker, I feel it may be of help to the House if I briefly touch on the background of individual payment of taxes in this country over the past 10 years. I do this because I feel a review of such figures reveals the absolutely staggering impact the Trudeau Liberal government has had upon individual taxpayers in the country. In many ways I feel that the income tax form we will be discussing today epitomizes the present government in office. It illustrates their glossing over of illegalities and, in some respects, their encouragement of dishonesty. It also illustrates their contempt for parliament and, in fact, the form, in its confused state, is the epitomy of the government, which itself is confused.
When Canadians finish paying the 1972 taxes which they will pay after filing the current form they, as individuals, will have paid in the aggregate in the five years since this government gained power some $38 billion. Under this government they will have paid an amount which is almost equal to the entire aggregate amount paid by all Canadian individuals in the previous 50 years. If you like, you can go back to Confederation, since the income tax legislation was introduced only in 1917. In short, this government has inflicted on Canadian
March 5, 1973

individual taxpayers, in the aggregate, as much taxation as has been inflicted in the previous 50 to 100 years.
It is important to remember that for 1972 it is likely that Canadian taxpayers in the aggregate will pay some $10 billion. That is almost five times as much as the individual taxpayers in this country paid in 1962, and it is almost two and a half times as much as was paid by individual taxpayers in 1967, the year before this government under this Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. This House should bear in mind that while Ministers of Finance such as Mr. Benson and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton)) have repeatedly mentioned that they have taken a certain number of people off the tax rolls, many more have gone on the tax rolls than have come off during this government's five years of rule. In fact, there are two million more people on the individual tax paying rolls today than there were five years ago. There are four million more than there were 10 years ago.
What is most disappointing is that, when we review the individual taxes paid by the average taxpayer in Canada, we find that in 1962 he paid $427; in 1967, he paid $646 and in 1972, he paid $1,176. If we put a deflater on those figures, we see they are equally alarming. Expressed in 1962 dollars, the average taxpayer in that year paid $427. In 1967 he paid $560. Today, and I emphasize, this is in terms of constant dollars, he is paying $841 into the federal treasury. That is an increase of 50 per cent since this government took office. We must bear that in mind as the background of the situation that faces the 10 million Canadian taxpayers who must now cope with the income tax form that we are reviewing today.
As I mentioned, we say that the form is confusing. It has been said that no man should have to pay a tax which he cannot reasonably be expected to understand. In this respect, the Department of National Revenue appears to agree. If we review their booklet Inside Taxation 1972, we find this statement in the introduction, and I quote:
-there is abundant evidence of a direct correlation between taxpayer understanding of the tax laws and procedures and the most efficient and economic administration of the tax-collecting function.
The introduction also makes the interesting comment that the word "taxation" is a Latin derivative which means to touch sharply. In many ways, there is a sharp touch on us today.
Hear, hear!

On the subject of confusion, there are many ways in which one can attempt to portray the anxiety felt by literally millions of Canadians today as they try to cope with this form. I think we should bear in mind that in the last taxation year for which figures are available, 80 per cent of those filing tax returns in Canada used the T-l short form. So, for approximately 80 per cent of our taxpayers in this current year the form distributed to them will be a completely new experience. When we compare it with the T-l short form with which they are familiar we find that whereas they had 74 blanks to fill in on the old form there are more than 300 to cope with in the new form. About $1 million is being spent on advertizing and promotions, in an attempt to convince individual tax-25789-47
Income Tax
payers that the form is not really as complicated as it looks. I would suggest, though, that the mere fact officials of the Department of National Revenue feel it necessary to spend this million dollars is proof that they know it is an extremely difficult form to cope with. I might mention that rate of tax schedules are appended to both the old and the new forms. But for reasons unknown to me in the one form the schedules show odd amounts whereas in the other, even amounts are shown. This tends to make it difficult for the average taxpayer to compare his current rate of taxation with rates in former years. Has this been done deliberately? I do not know.
I do know there has been tremendous pressure on regional offices of the Department of National Revenue as people seek to have their taxation position clarified. In my taxation area, Toronto, there are some 1,500,000 taxpayers whose forms will be processed through one office. I am told the department has increased its staff from 30 to 60 people who will deal at the front desk with inquiries from the 1,500,000 taxpayers. In other words, for every 25,000 taxpayers in my area there is one person to man the desk and iron out whatever difficulties might be experienced by taxpayers in coping with the new form.
Members of the public have been told, it is true, that they can telephone for assistance. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that before entering this debate today I asked my secretary to telephone the Toronto office to ask about the number of inquiries they were currently processing and whether the staff had actually been increased for this purpose. I am sorry to report that I cannot give the House this information, because after trying 25 times to get through on the telephone she gave up. Suppose I had wished to discuss a tax problem with that office in Toronto. I would still be waiting to get through so that I might have a chance of finding out the answer. At least, that would have been the position as at two o'clock.
Mr. Speaker, James H. Boren, the self-proclaimed president of the National Association of Professional Bureaucrats, thinks Canada's new tax system is so complicated that Washington would do well to adopt the same method. In explanation of his reason for making such a statement, Mr. Boren says:
I would say, almost without hesitation, that the tax forms epitomize our feelings about the maximum extension of retrogressive facilitation.
In other words, the new forms have achieved great success in complicating the already complicated. Later, Mr. Boren made the comment:
The guidelines are these. When in charge, ponder; when in trouble, delegate; when in doubt, mumble.
We have referred in our motion to the fact that the form as it now exists is in certain respects illegal. Hon. friends of mine will expand on this later in the debate. For example, provision is made for an age exemption which has not been approved by parliament. Provision is made for a deduction in respect of disability which has not been approved by parliament. Then again, there is provision made for a deduction in connection with education and this, too, has not been approved by parliament. In effect, we are asking some 10 million people to deal with this form knowing that parliamentary approval is still required before it is legal in certain respects. It was

March 5, 1973
Income Tax
unnecessary for this to have happened. We in the Progressive Conservative party asked repeatedly after the election that parliament be convened as early as possible so that matters such as those to which I have referred could have been dealt with and legalized.
I would also suggest that it is extremely unfair for the Minister of Finance to have adopted a philosophy which requires taxpayers to add to their income an amount they have never earned. I am referring to the fact that for the first time in connection with dividend income, taxpayers are expected to add to the amount they received in dividends an arbitrary one-third and count it as taxable income. It is unfair to ask any taxpayer to do this. In effect, he is being asked to report figures he knows are not true.
Granted, the public relations people, Fred Davis and others, have assured the public that the form is easier than it looks. But I suggest it is a very cruel thing to be telling ten million taxpayers in the country not to worry unless attention is drawn, at the same time, to a statement appearing just below the space left for signature, which reads: "It is a serious offence to make a false return".
I believe-and we have made this point in our motion, as well-that the government should extend financial assistance to help taxpayers cope with this form. Department of National Revenue officials admit that it costs approximately $10 to process each return. In short, it costs about $100 million to process the ten million forms with which they will be dealing. Surely it is not too much to expect that if the government feels it is necessary to spend $10 for their processing, it should assist the taxpayer who has to do the bulk of the work in preparing his return. Without such assistance I think it is fair to say that the government has imposed a further levy on the taxpayers of this country in the form of the amount the taxpayers will have to spend in completing their income tax returns. Assuming an amount of $10 per taxpayer, we are talking of a levy of $100 million, in addition to the taxation already levied upon them by the former Minister of Finance, Mr. Benson, and the present Minister of Finance.
In this context, I feel it is probably wise to remember that the individual taxpayers of this country are paying approximately one-half of the total revenue received by the federal treasury. In this connection, our proposal that there be an extension of time for taxpayers to complete their returns is only equitable in the circumstances. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of National Revenue has only 28 offices across the country to service taxpayers. As I have mentioned, some one and a half million taxpayers go through the Toronto area office alone. To expect the average taxpayer to file his return by April 30, with the small amount of assistance given him by existing departmental officers is extremely unfair.
Tied in with this is the broad subject of tax refunds. In the fiscal year ending March 31, 1972 those refunds amounted to approximately $866 million. It is anticipated that the figure will be approximately $1 billion in the current year. The government should do all in its power to expedite early repayment of those funds to our taxpayers.

The income tax form is so complex, so confusing, that one must ask oneself what was in the mind of the government when it prepared the form. I am more alarmed about this than perhaps anything else, because I believe that the government is setting up 10 million Canadians for further taxation of a kind that we in this House have not even thought of yet. I am told by those who have had some experience with the growth of this type of bureaucratic taxation, that in other countries it has been quite usual to introduce a very complicated form, then in subsequent years new taxes are imposed, such as a possession tax or, as suggested at one time in this House, a capital appraisal tax. Surely, we should recognize the possibility that the present government, if left in power for much longer, will introduce some such tax in order to extract even more from the average taxpayer of this country.
Let me also mention that the form is not only confusing to read but it is an extremely bulky document. As has been pointed out, the length of the form is some 13 feet if attached lengthwise page by page. Many do not realize that if these forms were stretched end to end they would cover a distance of almost 50,000 miles. In short, the forms would stretch twice around the world along its equator. To put it in the Canadian context, the forms could stretch from sea unto sea eight times and from north to south eight times, leaving lots of room for bows.
You really are stretching it.

This ribbon of paper symbolizes perhaps what the present government calls national unity. This ribbon of paper stretching from border to border, east to west and north to south, is what the government presumably feels is going to unite this country. It will unite it in utter frustration, confusion and indignation. I believe we should not tolerate this type of behaviour on the part of any government. A Progressive Conservative government would not have inflicted an income tax form like this upon the people of Canada. A Progressive Conservative government would indeed be expediting refunds at the present time to the taxpayers of Canada who rightfully can expect a refund. We believe it is high time that the government of Canada got the message that the taxpayers and voters of this country tried to give them in the last election. In short, Mr. Speaker, the government's time is up. The people of Canada want them no longer, and they want these tax forms no longer.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of speaking in this debate, but I am aware of the confusion that normally takes place at income tax time from my own point of view. A couple of items I received in my mail recently interested me. One was the Ontario property tax credit return, and I also received a farm tax return. I received several other things that I did not understand as well, so I decided to go down and get one of these kits from the post office. Even the first page of it is unintelligible, but it included the Ontario property tax form, and having read the first page of it I am sure I do not know how it will affect me as a farmer, which I am not. Neither am I sure how it will affect me as a property owner. As a result, I am not at all sure what I am going to do with the two little forms I received from the Ontario government; if they had kept them it would have made it
March 5, 1973

far simpler for me. The more you read this sheaf of paper, the more confused you become and the less able you are to fill out your return.
The other day a man wrote me on behalf of his daughter complaining about the complexity of this form. After looking at the form I realized why he was confused. This woman has two children, one of pre-school age and one who goes to school. She works in the local hospital as a nurse, most of the time on day shift, although not always. She has to be at work at 7.30 in the morning. She hires one of the neighbour's children, a 16 year old girl, to come in and give the children their breakfast and get them ready for school. The one who stays at home is looked after by the lady next door. The young 16 year old girl takes the other child to school. That is the end of her part in the routine.
The one child comes home from school on her own and goes to the neighbour's house where the younger child is and has her lunch. The first child takes the second child to kindergarten and then she goes to school. This does not end the matter because the children both come home after school. Then, another 16 year old girl looks after them until the mother arrives home. Occasionally, this woman has to work overtime or has to work a swing shift. This does not happen often, but it does further complicate the matter.
The complaint is that the 16 year old girls involved do not make contributions to the Canada Pension Plan and do not work the minimum time which would require them to pay unemployment insurance. The minister may know where in this form you enter contributions to unemployment insurance as an employer, or Canada Pension contributions. I am not sure where it is and I do not intend to search for it now as that would lengthen my speech considerably. If you do not enter these items you cannot claim expenses for your housekeeper or your babysitters.
The woman to whom I referred could not possibly set up the bookkeeping system required to look after these things. The cost would not warrant keeping track of the unemployment insurance or Canada Pension Plan contributions for these girls who work two hours some days, an hour and a half some other days and perhaps not at all on other occasions. The woman might just as well go on welfare in the first place, and she might well be driven to that position as a result of a mental breakdown before she completes this tax form, and that is only the housekeeper section. I see no reason why this could not be simplified.
I now look at the second page, which apparently is for people who can legally cheat the government. There are all kinds of exemptions listed here including medical expenses and charitable donations. Anyone I know who has medical expenses also probably has a medical plan and, therefore, does not have any expenses as such. It is true that my doctor charges me more than the scheme will pay, but that is a small amount and I am not sure that you should list it here.
There are spaces here for capital dispositions which include personal use of property, listed personal property, other capital properties, real estate, bonds and other properties, and there is a place also for a summary of capital
25789-47J
Income Tax
gains. Presumably these all apply to the rich. Perhaps if you looked through it you would find a place to deduct as an expense the cost of having an accountant look after this for you. Of course, this part will not have any interest for the average taxpayer who will be paying a comparatively small amount. I do not see included in this form a place for deducting that expense paid in respect of child care.
When we included child care expenses as a deduction for income tax purposes, we thought this would be a fairly simple thing for the mother who got herself a job and had to hire someone to look after her children. I find it is not simple. As is pointed out in this schedule, you must have the security number of those individuals for whom you are claiming an expense. It states here that you should not include payments made to a relative under the age of 21 at any time in 1972, or payments made to a person claimed as a dependent by you or by your spouse. It also states that if payments were made to a boarding school or camp, you cannot include any part of such payment in excess of $15 per week per child. Below that there are spaces for the names and addresses and individual social security numbers of those to whom payments were made. The woman to whom I referred has made great effort to provide for her children and now is not going to be able to claim these expenses.
I presume we are trying to cover all tax bases. It may be that the 16 year old girl who comes in in the morning and gives these children their breakfast, getting the one ready to go to school and the other to the neighbour's house, should be paying income tax, should have a social security number and be eligible for benefits. I presume that is the justification. If she did pay income tax it would be such a small amount it would not pay to operate the computer, and the money would obviously be returned. I am sure if she made a contribution to the Canada Pension Plan this whole thing would prove to be a nuisance and not feasible.
I do not agree with those people who are always complaining about changes in society, because I think changes are necessary and are usually good, but I am not sure that the changes in this tax form will work to the benefit of those people with whom I am used to dealing, the people earning $5,000 to $10,000 per year. They pay their income tax and they are allowed deductions for their wives and children. In addition, they get the $100 deduction for medical expenses and the other small deductions provided by the minister. They will be allowed those deductions and no more. Most people will not fill up those spaces provided for contributions. People who make contributions to the church usually do so on a regular cash basis rather than by cheque.
My father was a very meticulous person and had some knowledge of the income tax field, being in charge of a section of the Department of Agriculture during the war. This was the economic section of that department. I was always amazed when he made a contribution to the church that he made it by cheque. He knew exactly what to do with that contribution. As a miner, on the other hand, when I made a contribution to a charitable organization I just gave it the money. Probably I would have spent it for something else, so I can never remember being

March 5, 1973
Income Tax
interested in getting a receipt. Charitable donations were never used for income tax purposes because I really did not have too much money to throw around anyway. In those days the form was fairly simple and I could fill it out myself.
I suggest the form could be much simpler for people whose earnings are through wages and whose deductions are made on a payroll basis. In such cases, the amount of the income tax payment is deducted and is entered on the T4 slip. It should be necessary merely to include the personal exemptions and that would be all there would be to it. I never understood why there was not a calculation which would vary from province to province. I do not understand why my Ontario provincial tax is not figured out for me. If the province of Manitoba, for example, should have a different tax structure, a different form could be used for that province. From my point of view this would solve a good part of the problem. It seems to me many people in this country do not have any unusual deductions or unusual sources of income. In their case it is a straight matter of showing the amount of wages, the exemptions, the charitable donations and so on. Such a person should be able to use a tax schedule and simply determine the amount he must pay or the amount of refund he might have. I do not understand why it should be made any more complicated.
I see no reason that people in the lower income groups who would have no right-offs should have to be involved with such a complicated form. All this does is show a person who is a wage earner employed in John Blow's plant that there are other people in this society who are entitled to many tax deductions to which he is not entitled. It shows him where the rip-off comes in so far as other people are concerned. These are not available to him, and yet he must become mixed up in the whole problem without receiving any of the benefits. When I became a Member of Parliament my income increased slightly, by about $1,000. In those days, I found that the amount of $1,000 placed me in a category that was not in the table. Therefore, I had to work out the calculation. I went to high school and learned how to make mathematical calculations. However, it had been a long time since I was at school and I found it very difficult to come up with an answer. I had considerable difficulty when my income increased from $5,000 to $6,000.
What about now?

Now, I am not even sure what it is. From looking at this form it would seem that I may have income of which I am not aware. That small cheque I received as a rebate in respect of my farm must be income from somewhere. It is interesting to look at this mauve form for the province of Ontario. Perhaps if I study this form I might understand why I got this money back. Mr. Speaker, I believe there surely could be a much simpler system. My income is shown on my T4 slip. If I should be unemployed I would have to have a TU-1 slip. However, if I am fully employed, earning a salary and the deductions are taken off at source, my salary is shown on the T4 slip. In such a situation I should be able to do a simple calculation and determine my income tax. This form is very com-

plicated. I cannot even understand the first page. Then, there is this Ontario property tax. I suppose that is in respect of my house.
Send it back.
Do not bother filling it out.

The amount I received in respect of the farm is a very small amount. I would gladly send it back, because no doubt it will just confuse matters. The other day I received a T4 slip indicating I had received a relatively small sum of money in the form of a dividend from an insurance policy. I always thought that would be included each year and totalled at the end. I never drew any money; it accumulated. I did not realize I would have to make a payment on something I was not receiving. I will never receive it. I would have to die in order to receive it.
I agree with the Conservative who moved this motion when he stated that this was a complicated form.
Hear, hear!

The minister may say it is not. I do not know what his profession was, but I would be very happy to take these blank forms over to him and have him fill them out while he makes his speech. I would be very surprised if he could fill them out in time for you, Mr. Speaker, not to call him to order. I believe there should be two things. First, there should be a tax form which would include the provincial tax, so that each person would receive a form which would indicate the amount of his provincial tax rather than requiring that he make a separate calculation.
There is no question that this complicated form is necessary for anyone engaged in the business field. Probably there is another one relating to farmers which is probably four times as complicated. I suggest, however, that there should be a very simple, uncomplicated form on which the average person would need only show the deductions to which he is entitled and the information on his T4 slip.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired.
He has not completed his income tax form yet.

Mr. Speaker, as I can see, this motion gives an indication of the complexity of the tax forms to be filled by the Canadian taxpayers who must comply with the requirements of the tax system.
According to the wording of the motion, the government's income tax return forms will lead to confusion. It will not be the first time. Considering the double taxation system that too many people support, knowingly or not, we find that tax itself is being taxed. Indeed, the provincial tax taxes the federal tax; that is not very intelligent but that is the way it is.
The motion before us refers to illegality. It would be interesting indeed to witness a legal argument in order to
March 5, 1973

establish the legality or illegality of the tax return forms. Such are the consequences of a crazy system according to which wealth is being appraised in the form of dollars instead of things, property and other real values.
We also note that the motion calls upon the government to give harassed taxpayers-it has been found that the taxpayers were harassed, and better late than never- financial aid and an extension of time and it adds "to expedite payment of tax refunds".
Considering the object of this motion was to prevent confusion, I believe the wording somewhat lacks clarity.
The idea naturally is to keep advocating an outmoded system while at the same time trying to convince most hon. members that the motion should be supported, without suggesting anything practical to lighten the burden of the so-called harassed taxpayers. It is obvious that tax return forms should be at least written in a more simple and clearer language to avoid high expenses for accounting services.
The government seems to like to create complications for taxpayers with complicated income tax return forms. We see that all year long, particularly at the end of the month of April or during the month of May. A lot of income tax problems are submitted to me each week and have to do with the difficulties the taxpayers face in trying to comply with government requirements.
It is not necessary to spend hours studying the legislation to discover how stupid are most of the laws governing the country. Everything is so oriented as to protect the money system instead of intelligently distributing the existing wealth.
We find that thousands of public servants paid from tax moneys are watching the taxpayers. Interesting indeed but this is what you find. If we keep on using this method we will find ourselves in the absurb situation where half the Canadians will be watching the other half.
I admit that we must have laws and regulations. However, I am under the impression that the complexity of existing laws has contributed to creating a stampede attitude within a disastrous economic situation. Our financial system supported by too many of our "colored" politicians has contributed to create a wolf mentality where everyone is running after the almighty dollar-the symbol of the wealth kept too rare by those controlling it-with the result that many laws are violated, many formalities are not fulfilled, many regulations are not enforced, and this is contributing to maintain a riot atmosphere which the government is often obliged to quell through emergency measures.
Those at the controls always find good reasons to justify the resulting tax increases and formalities. And yet it is easy to understand that the after-tax money left to the taxpayer may be spent as he pleases, whereas the tax money is spent as the state sees fit and not as the individual does.
The higher the income earmarked for taxes-whatever formality used-the more the we steer toward state socialism so that if the government took everything, individuals would pay nothing themselves and everything would be paid by the government. This would be absolute state socialism.

I would like to quote part of an editorial broadcast by CFCM-TV station on June 1, 1967. Speaking of popular democracies, the editorialist mentioned something thought-provoking, and I quote:
In those countries personal incomes have been over-taxed to such an extent that the cost of living index has wildly spiraled, with no compensation whatever by way of an equivalent increase in incomes. The February 1967 report on international financial statistics indicates that in Yugoslavia the cost of living, increased by 167 per cent from 1958 to 1966, whereas the index of incomes is unchanged. According to the same report, in Sweden, a country governed by a socialist government and benefiting from a mixed economic system, the cost of living has gone up by 34 per cent during the past six years. This increase, to a large extent, is due to the burden of social measures and overtaxation.
It makes no difference what method they use.
This should cause everyone to ponder, and specially those who want to drive us to socialism.
Yet, the individual is paramount and governments are merely institutions at his service.
Others complain specially about taxes, feeling that they are being deprived of the fruit of their toil. They are perfectly right. But what we want to stress is that the increase in taxes is a rapid progression towards state socialism. Moreover, when private enterprise, over-taxed, loses heart, it is necessarily replaced by an industrial or a state monopoly: the first means domination through money, the second means domination with the all-encompassing government. A system has to be very sick indeed when the only choice is between two ways of enslaving individuals.
There is another solution: control funds at the source, in keeping with the facts, the individual's rights and the country's potential. This would mean Social Credit.
But, there, people do hesitate. And our governments would rather control the individuals and leave alone the privileges of the people who create money.
We are living in a world where many seem to have lost a sense of balance, of duty and of responsibility, no matter what forms are being used.
In fact, nowadays, we find that millions of dollars are spent to support exploration trips to the moon, whereas millions of citizens, on our planet, lack the necessities of life, despite the means at our disposal to house, clothe and feed human beings properly. We are grappling with a situation of that kind.
Among the people responsible for this state of affairs, we can easily count many politicians who, in my opinion, do a poor job as far as the interests of the citizens are concerned. Instead of taking the time of the House to discuss red tape due to a silly system, we should rather try to find some means of altering the system which is responsible for all those insignificant and complicated formalities, legal or illegal. We are driven to such a situation by the very nature of the system. Therefore, let us instead try to find a means for changing the silly system that rules us.
Often more interested in showing off than pleasing people, many politicians today are playing the role of actors in offices that would rather command some com-

prehensive legislation to meet men's needs. I admit that there are good men in all parties-
And also women!

Yes, a few. I admit, again, that there are good men in all political parties at the present time as there were in the past. However, they seem to be paralyzed by completely out of date procedures.
I cannot find a logical explanation for the fact that after so many years of administrative experience, application of plans, studies and suggestions of all kinds, the working and agricultural people of Canada are now at grips with problems of unemployment, insecurity and debts. And more serious still, this kind of unbearable and demoralizing situation for many people created a feeling of revolt which contributes to produce a climate of insecurity.
No one will deny the fact that the number of criminals increases seriously in a country upon which Providence has bestowed all kinds of wealth.
How come our learned politicians, or at least those who think they are, still prefer to keep procedures which lead to such results.
A group of politicians of a certain colour have come to believe that a country whose leaders succeed in paying interest on the public debt may be considered as being well administered. Imagine what would happen if all Canadians took this position. And yet we in Canada should give the example. These people have the gall to come and speak to us about a balanced budget, while they only succeeded in creating a financial and economic situation that is completely-
