speechtext: The Chair heard the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) mention formalities and complexities a moment or so ago, and assumed that this was in reference to the matter of the income tax forms that we are debating. However, perhaps the hon. member should bear in mind the somewhat limited nature of the debate we are embarked upon today. The hon. member for Kamouraska.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to explain my views on that subject.
At the beginning of my remarks, I explained quite clearly the meaning of the motion, I think, and today I notice that an hon. member is blaming me for speaking a little
too much about the system or about different systems. I shall point out to him, and this is very important, that the stupid formalities we are discussing derive from a foolish system that the hon. member is supporting. That is the reason!
I do not think I am straying from the subject matter because I think those formalities would not be necessary if we had a logical system. It is because we have a confusing system that we have confusing formalities and we try by all kinds of means to set things straight. Each year, reforms are made about these forms; it is such a complicated matter that taxpayers are forced to spend hundreds of dollars in accountant offices to have these famous forms filled, forms which are created by the foolish system the hon. member is supporting. This is the reality and I am glad to have the opportunity to say it in the House this afternoon.
What is your system?

What? Our system? We have a system of common sense. It recommends a distribution of goods based on an orderly financial system and not a financial system which has to admit-I said it earlier-that as long as the country can administer himself by paying the interest on its debt, it can consider itself as being well administered. Have you ever seen such a concept of administration? Would an industrial, a farmer or anybody else who would administer his budget in Canada simply by being satisfied with paying the interest on his debts be considered an able administrator? A foolish system brings the formalities we have. Then we try to bring about improvements in the formalities of application, not only in the area of income tax, but in lots of other areas. There are administrative procedures which are almost inapplicable. I could cite lots of examples that demonstrate it very clearly, but the Income Tax Act is probably the most eloquent.
So I continue my comments, for I think they are quite timely and yet some of them were not in my text.
You had better stick to your text.

I understand that in the system there can be major reasons to levy a tax. When it comes to providing a service requested by the community and there is no way to provide it without depriving some members of that community, this can be understood, but if there is a way to provide that service without depriving anyone, it is not fair to deprive citizens of what they own.
If I take my neighbour's money, this is a theft. When the government takes the taxpayers' money, what is it called? An individual is not allowed to take another individual's property. And the government could do it. Taxes can, besides, reach so high a level, so heavily burden farmers or manufacturers that they discourage personal initiative.
This is verified. Any legislation whose objective is to tax contains sections to tax capital gains and other gains. However, I have not found in all the tax laws, even in the heavy Bill C-259 which contains 740 pages, a single section providing for a compensation for those who would experience losses instead of profits. Everything is organized to

March 5, 1973

protect the financial system and nothing is provided to compensate the victims.
I do not think that changing the forms would bring much relief; it is mainly the system that needs to be changed.
Taxes do not disturb only those they hit, they disturb the whole community because they sabotage production, just as the whole system does.
There is another way of getting money. It would be to simply take back the manufacturing power presently in the hands of chartered banks. But we really have to want it though.
Who must be in charge of creating money and distributing it where it is needed if not the sovereign government which should be the only one so authorized? A government not doing so deserves to be called "the servant of private interests", and you know where I read that expression.
Instead of adopting a tax method which produces provoking and complicated forms, if the government were to use its sovereign power to restore order in the monetary system, it would be possible to balance the incomes of people instead of taking away from them the gains they have made. And there would be no need for forms because the worker would keep the money he earned.
Those who always come up with the word "inflation" would already be anxious to know how long a government could do that. I would say without hesitation: as long as that brings good without evil. There is no doubt that it could follow that method for as long as certain means of production are unutilized.
Presently, production is far from being what it should be in Canada. There are a lot of unemployed-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but the time allotted to him has expired. The hon. Minister of National Revenue.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Stanbury (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the lot of the tax collector is not a happy one. It never has been and is not likely to be. Paying taxes and completing the various forms required to do so are not the most enjoyable responsibilities of citizenship. Especially at this time of year, taxpayers are seldom moved to thoughts or words of fulsome praise and thanksgiving for the tax collector as he goes about his appointed task. Therefore, we were not surprised to hear that this subject was to be the basis of the opposition motion today, particularly in view of the time spent recently on this subject by opposition spokesmen-who have not always spoken with the greatest accuracy, I must say.
I enjoyed, as I always do, listening to my hon. friend from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). Knowing him as I do, I found many echoes in his speech of his career as a reporter, lawyer, farmer and financeer. He knows the value of publicity and how to get it. He knows the value of a picture like the one which appeared in the press not long ago showing him draped in forms, schedules and tables, all taped together. He knows full well that not even he, nor
Income Tax
any one of his constituents, would have to use all of them. Actually, when I first saw the picture of the hon. member in the newspaper with these forms, I thought he was displaying a collection of old stock certificates.
He supported his motion with "lawyerly" logic, demonstrating that legal training has equipped him to make much of little. In what he has produced here today, he has rivalled the sheep that roam on and enrich the fields of his country estate. His sheep, however, would know better than to produce that in the House of Commons.
It was a very woolly speech.

It was not a serious speech and this is not a serious motion, Mr. Speaker. This motion has been thrown in while the Tories play for time, trying their best to brew up a motion for tomorrow which will not veer too far from any principles they have left and will appeal at the same time sufficiently to socialists and those with Social Credit tastes. They are trying to devise the means, not to improve any law or any program, but simply to destroy this government and this parliament. They are doing this to satisfy their hunger for power. So, today they are taking up the valuable time of parliament playing with form, and with forms, instead of contributing to the constructive improvement of the substance of our laws and programs.
This is political gamesmanship of an old and stale style. It is being played at the expense of ordinary taxpayers, giving them a false impression that may inhibit their taking advantage of tax benefits available to them.
That is not just my opinion, Mr. Speaker. Ralph Erring-ton, reporting on Radio Station CFRB and other stations a week or so ago, said:
Conservative MP's, and to a lesser degree some New Democrats, have been waging a steady campaign to convince the public that the new tax forms are so complicated that it would take a team of chartered accountants to complete the returns. So it was with some misgivings that this reporter decided, as usual, to do my own accounting, and file my tax return without any outside help. Ninety minutes later, my calculations were completed and rechecked, the tax form typed out and stuffed in an envelope ready for mailing. Needless to say, this haste is due to the fact that I've got some money coming back. If anything, the new tax forms were easier to complete than previous ones, with assistance from an easy-to-follow instruction booklet. Granted, anyone with investment income, capital gains to report or working on a selfemployed or commission basis no doubt would need the help of an accountant. But these people would seek professional help anyway. To those politicians who say the average salaried taxpayer can't complete his own tax return, I say: 'Rubbish!' As Fred Davis says in the Revenue Department ads: 'It's easier than it looks.'
That is the opinion of an independent and respected journalist of the parliamentary press gallery.
Giving me a hard time as the minister is "fair ball". I expected it when I took this job. However, I appeal to the members of the Official Opposition not to hurt the little people, the low and middle income earners, the average citizens. I say to those members through you, Mr. Speaker, restrain your ambitions; do not try to climb to power on the backs of our average citizens by stampeding them into fear of our tax forms, into fear of taking advantage of

March 5, 1973
Income Tax
benefits and, perhaps, undermining the self-assessment approach on which our income tax system is based.
We should remind ourselves that our Canadian system of self-assessment is by far the most democratic, the most efficient and the most economical means of collecting taxes. If I had enough time at my disposal I could refer to the views of tax authorities in other jurisdictions to the effect that the administration of our system, as it has evolved over the years under several administrations, is a model of fairness and efficiency. As other ministers responsible for my portfolio before me have done, I conceive it as my responsibility to maintain and improve our self-assessment system. If we are to maintain and improve it, we must administer tax legislation fairly, uniformly and impartially as well as with efficiency and courtesy.
Self-assessment is the exercise of a fundamental relationship between the citizens and their government. The declaration of income, the claiming of deductions, the calculation of tax and the use of an accessible and objective appeal process are all acts of civil participation second only in importance, I suggest, to the exercise of the electoral franchise. But, Mr. Speaker, rights involve obligations. The fulfilment of obligations can be inconvenient. I do not derive any pleasure from assembling records and filling out an income tax form. The keeping of records, the calculation of deductions and, generally, the completion of returns are an inconvenience, and I will not disagree if anyone suggests that is an understatement.
For my part, I know that the taxation component of my department makes every effort to minimize the task it imposes on taxpayers through forms and procedural requirements. It is simply common sense that we do that. Apart from our concern for the taxpayer, the difficulties he or she encounters and the errors he or she makes in the return are time consuming and costly for the department. So, Mr. Speaker, it alarms me when certain interests and certain individuals, in pursuit of personal gain or for other selfish reasons, prey on the natural apprehension of taxpayers at a time of change, caring not for the interests of the individual taxpayer nor for the integrity of our self-assessment system. Also, it disturbs me that the Official Opposition would dignify some of these views and claims that are misleading and even false, certainly not motivated by concern for taxpayers at large or the maintenance of our system of taxation.
They display political cynicism.

May I quote the words of another respected commentator, Mr. Speaker? Writing in the Calgary Herald, Ken Hull said of the current tax form: "smart money would bet that any puppy could lick it to death". He went on to say:
Anyone who mastered last year's tax form will find it a pushover-assuming he or she hasn't had a 1,400 per cent salary increase; bought or sold half of Saskatchewan; become the major shareholder of Imperial Oil, or sold part of his Rolls Royce fleet.
Because of the many reckless statements about the complexity of the paper work that were voiced by certain persons even before they had actually seen the revised form, we suggested to taxpayers that they should not prejudge the forms and the new guide before they had an
[Mr. Stanbury.l
opportunity to read them. We tried to acquaint taxpayers with the expanded and improved services available to them in our 28 district taxation offices.
Some have attacked our efforts to inform and encourage citizens in this essential process of democracy, although I might express my appreciation for the fact the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) wants our information program extended. The cost of this program is approximately 4.5 cents per capita, but there is accumulating evidence that it is paying off for the taxpayers. Citizens who have been turned off, so to speak, by ill-informed and irresponsible criticism have been reassured and have found that it is no more difficult for most people to cope with the new return than with previous ones. That is all we have claimed, Mr. Speaker. Not that it is not complicated or difficult, as I suppose all tax forms are, but that it is easier than it looks. Joe McClelland wrote in the London Free Press, and I quote:
For the past year we've been assailed from all quarters with dire and gloomy declarations that the umpteen pages of the new tax return are incontestably beyond the capacity of any ordinary mortal to fathom.
Later in his column he concluded:
-this one is the easiest return I've grappled with in 15 years or more.
Some hon. Members; Hear, hear!

Why do those independent observers say this? This year we had one tax form for every taxpayer. It is a four-page tax form, not what some of the critics would like it to be. In the envelope also is a guide which gives simple step-by-step instructions for completing the return. Also included are tax tables to assist in calculation and a set of schedules, some of which some taxpayers require in support of their return.
The page size of this year's return is smaller. It is the equivalent of one page shorter than last year's T1 General form and one and one-half pages longer than last year's T1 Short. If those taxpayers who formerly filed on a T1 Short ignore those areas of the form devoted to selfemployed earnings, as they are asked to do, their form this year is only slightly longer than last year, the difference being almost entirely due to the addition of unemployment insurance premiums as a deduction, and a more open layout in the identification and tax calculation areas on page one, which makes it easier for taxpayers to complete that page.
There has been so much misrepresentation that I want to go into some detail. The tax tables this year have been expanded to serve those with taxable incomes up to $12,000, the cut-off formerly being $8,000. This expansion greatly reduces the number of taxpayers having to complete the detailed tax calculation schedule, which is even more apparent when one takes into account the increase in taxable income due to larger exemptions.
There are eight schedules other than the detailed tax calculation schedule. Of these, four are virtually identical to those which accompanied last year's T1 General form and will be used by the same people who would have used them last year. Of the remaining four, one is simply a printed schedule for use by those who would have had to
March 5, 1973

create their own in previous years. Another removes from the tax form a little-used section for additional personal exemption. The remaining two schedules concerning capital dispositions and child care expenses are new. In addition, for residents of Ontario and Manitoba, there are forms on which they may apply for a credit against their municipal property taxes. I sometimes agree with the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) that it might have been easier if we had not served as the mailman for these provincial governments.
Hear, hear!

We estimate that approximately five million taxpayers will not have to use any schedules at all. It is expected that for approximately 80 per cent of the taxpayers, the only major new forms requirement is the small section on unemployment insurance premiums.
Why does everyone receive the same tax form? The spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party said that his party would not have shown this kind of consideration to the Canadian people. We could have decided not to send anybody any schedules, but rather send them scurrying out to the post offices to try to find the ones they need. Taxpayers could have been spared the sight of all that paper, but a substantial number who required one or more schedules would have been put to the inconvenience of applying to a taxation office or a post office for those they needed. Why were the Short and General forms combined this year? The use of two forms presumed a considerable difference in the requirements of the groups receiving each form, and that it was possible to get the right form to the right people.
It was felt that neither of these presumptions were strongly enough indicated to warrant separate forms this year. Equity also entered the picture, since experience in other countries as well as in Canada suggested that abbreviated forms lead to taxpayers overlooking or ignoring possible exemptions and benefits to which they are entitled. We do not want them to miss any of those, Mr. Speaker. It may be of interest to hon. members that before making the decision to use one form we consulted our Tax Advisory Committee which is made up of knowledgeable tax experts from across the country who volunteer their services and meet periodically with my officials to discuss departmental policies and procedures. That committee fully approved the change.
There has been a major effort, quite unjustified, to condemn the forms and guide in a way that might cause some taxpayers to throw up their hands and spend money unnecessarily for professional assistance. I do not have anything against professional help. That is a decision for any taxpayer. However, I must protest the innuendoes that our forms and guides are forcing taxpayers to engage outside help when they were able to cope with the filing requirements the past few years.
Tax reform was the subject of public discussion for almost 10 years. There was a good deal of controversy up to and since the parliamentary passage of Bill C-259 in December 1971. We were well aware that many taxpayers would be apprehensive in approaching their first tax reform return. We understood that and were prepared for it.
Income Tax
However, there have been a number of other circumstances that have exacerbated the normal apprehension. There have been some who did not agree with certain tax reform changes who have been using the tax form as an object of a rearguard action. Of course, they have a right to disagree, but I deplore the fact that they have tried, unsuccessfully, I believe, to undermine our self-assessment system.
While the administration of the Income Tax Act is often construed to mean collecting every cent the law permits, my department is equally concerned with collecting not one cent more than the law requires. We try to protect the taxpayers' interest in this regard in two basic ways: by correcting any errors or omissions we can in the assessment of returns, and by informing the taxpayers of provisions of the law that can work to their advantage.
Hon. members will be interested to know, I am sure, that in routine assessing action on last year's returns, we decreased the tax payable for more than 1,400,000 taxpayers by a total amount of more than $75 million. These decreases were effected unilaterally as a result of painstaking scrutiny and computer calculation in the Department of National Revenue.
In addition to protecting taxpayers from their own errors, considerable effort has been made to inform people of the benefits the law holds for taxpayers, and to help them avoid time consuming errors. As you may be aware, following the passage of tax reform legislation my department issued a series of explanatory pamphlets on various aspects of the new laws. More than 25 million copies of these pamphlets are in the hands of Canadians. Also, a comprehensive series of videotaped training courses were made available to tax practitioners and professionals. Almost 10,000 have taken advantage of these courses since May, 1972.
To handle the complex questions which arose for individuals contemplating transactions under the new tax laws, my department instituted an informal consultation service last year as a complement to the advance ruling service which had been available previously. More than
45,000	queries were handled by this service, 3,000 of which involved situations sufficiently complex as to require clearance through head office on special direct lines installed for that very purpose.
To handle inquiries from taxpayers now completing the tax returns, we have taken several fundamental steps. The first of these was to submit our staff to special training courses to enable them to anticipate and solve quickly and courteously any taxpayer problems brought to their attention. Second, we drastically increased the number of staff and requisite facilities for dealing with taxpayer inquiries. Third, and perhaps most important of all, we have put the expertise of the tax department at the disposal of every Canadian, no matter where he lives, by virtue of the new ZENITH 0-4000 telephone number.
That's a constructive way to handle it.

To assist taxpayers who cannot call during normal working hours, we have extended tele-
1896

March 5, 1973
Income Tax
phone inquiry service Monday and Tuesday evenings until 8 p.m. In all these actions, we have anticipated, and are prepared to handle efficiently, almost a 100 per cent increase in the normal taxpayer inquiries we receive during the filing season.
I have already touched on our information program which includes, besides advertising, various projects involving the print, radio and television media, speeches, tax education materials, special programs for groups such as older people, and so forth. Not all the programs of taxpayer assistance have originated from my department. I am particularly pleased to see the amount and quality of support which is coming from outside groups-newspapers, accountants and other professionals, senior citizens associations, neighbourhood action committees, service clubs and a host of other organizations have pitched in to inform and offer free services to taxpayers during this transitional period. I want to compliment them and congratulate them on behalf of the government. They have demonstrated that there are many people in Canada who do not expect the government to do everything for them. I expect that applies to most people.
Hear, hear!

Such has been the quality of this much-appreciated assistance, along with the efforts of my department, that I feel quite secure in asserting that never before has a legislative act of this House been the subject of such massive public study and public information.
All these efforts have been appreciated. I know, because I have heard from a large number of people to that effect.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, if taxpayers are as confused and so harassed, as the opposition claims today, one would expect a substantial increase in taxpayer errors in the filing of returns. While we have only just passed the deadline for employers to distribute T4 slips to their employees, and though the bulk of returns will be filed in future weeks, I can report to the House that errors in early returns up to last week were approximately 3 per cent less than at the comparable time last year.
Hear, hear!

I can also tell the House that a check of our district offices last week indicated that the vast majority of questions by taxpayers were in no way related to the alleged complexity of the form. Some 90 per cent of the telephone calls in one Ontario city for five days last week concerned the province's property tax credit, and nearly 50 per cent of the calls in all our Ontario and Manitoba offices during that period were inquiries about the property tax credit programs of the provinces.
Hear, hear!

During last weekend, when I heard of the intention of the opposition to move this motion, I just happened to read the lead editorial in the current issue of the Financial Post, the "bible" so often quoted by the opposition.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: What?

I do not have time to quote it all, but I should at least quote the first paragraph because it is extremely relevant to the motion before us. It reads:
Much emotional and irresponsible rhetoric has poured forth about the new income tax return. The fact is, the return is not all that complicated and the Department of National Revenue may be right that it's going to be easier than you think.
The newspaper went on to quote a prominent Toronto accountant as saying:
The form is not complicated. Furthermore, the guide which accompanies it is a masterpiece. It's the best guide I've seen anywhere.
Hear, hear!

I do not want to go on at great length. I do, however, want to tell hon. members that this year, as in past years, I am sure, the prime aim of the Minister of National Revenue and his department is not simply to collect the revenues which are necessary to carry out the program of the government-or which would be necessary to carry out the program of any government under a democratic system. Our first and foremost aim is to see that the people of Canada are well served by their income tax system; that every taxpayer makes the most of tax reform and the benefits arising from Liberal budgets in the past few years. We want the people of Canada to take every advantage to which they are entitled under the law. Citizens of Canada can depend on us to see that the law is administered in the most sensitive way and that some
7,700,000	Canadians who will be entitled to refunds this year get them as rapidly as this House permits by the passage of legislation.

I was wondering whether the minister would allow me to ask a question and, if so, whether he could give me an answer. I have asked him a couple of questions during the question period and he has been unable or unwilling to answer.
Order!

When he did not
answer one of my questions he did send me a letter-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Ask your question.
-asking me whether I had any further ideas on his crystal clear income tax guide and whether I would submit them to him.
Order!
I am wondering whether it is the policy of the government to ask us for our ideas.

I am very glad the hon. member asked about this. There was another member who the other day, asked a question in a rather sarcastic way. He wanted to know why I should be asking hon. members in the opposition for suggestions. I think this reaction demonstrates better than anything how a Conservative government would operate. They are so arrogant they do not care anything about anyone else's ideas.

Hear, hear!
March 5, 1973

I have heard a great deal in this House over the last few months about how perfidious this form is, but I have not received one constructive suggestion from hon. members opposite. And I do not expect to get one.
Hear, hear!

I wonder whether, before he sits down, the minister would comment on the assertion in the motion before us today, an assertion which has been repeated by at least one speaker, that the 1972 income tax forms which Canadians are now filling in are illegal. I believe there were references to the fact that there were certain points on which the income tax form differed from the Income Tax Act, and that we would not want people to fill out the form feeling that there was going to be a comeback because the law does not yet conform with the income tax form. I believe there is something about the authority that the minister has to prescribe such forms, but would he comment on the matter so that the confusion on this point will be cleared up?
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The tax forms are prescribed by the minister under section 150(1) and section 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. There is no question of their legality.
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Does that mean, for example, that where the form says that persons over 65 can deduct $1,000 rather than the $650 provided by the act, that is perfectly legal?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I really do not think it is in order for an hon. member to ask for what seems to me to be a legal opinion of the ministry. Is the hon. member rising on a question of privilege?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on a point of order.
Mr. Speaker, if it is not proper for the minister to comment on legal questions, is it proper for us to be debating a motion which indicates there is something before us that is illegal?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was hoping that the minister would seize the nettle himself. Perhaps he could be permitted to reply, since there are several million Canadians no doubt waiting upon his answer.

I had better not attempt a legal opinion for the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, but may I say that persons are being asked to fill out forms that are authorized by law. There are certain aspects of the budget of last May that the Minister of Finance has indicated he would like the House to deal with at an early date. There is no difficulty about having people complete forms according
Income Tax
to the form prescribed by the Minister of National Revenue, and they are proceeding to do this. I suppose about one million Canadians have already submitted their returns, and many of these have received a refund. Those who would qualify for a higher refund or a refund resulting from the budget measures of May 8 will, I hope, not have much longer to wait than the others.

That is right, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of National Revenue has indicated that he had not had one single thought or idea to help him from the members on this side.

This House, noting that the Government's income tax return forms are both confusing and illegal, calls upon the Government to give financial aid and an extension of time to harassed taxpayers, to expedite payment of tax refunds to more than six million taxpayers, and to take immediate steps to legalize both the 1972 tax structure and the forms.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INCOME TAX-SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FILING FORMS AND LEGALIZATION OF 1972 STRUCTURE AND FORMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most interested in the opening remarks of the minister concerning the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and what he described as sheep. We are more concerned about
1898

March 5, 1973
Income Tax
the fleecing of the people of Canada by the minister than we are about sheep. Apparently the minister is full of wool, or has that in mind. We are not just playing with forms in this debate but talking about equity. We are talking about the people of Canada receiving equity in taxation, the equity that the so-called tax reform legislation was supposed to give them. Now, with this conglomeration of blue, white and in some cases mauve pieces of paper, the taxpayers are not being given equity but a monstrous headache. This headache, together with the accounting cost Canadians have to bear and the problems confronting Canadian business, wipe out any attempt the act makes to treat Canadians equitably, and indeed creates more problems than the equity the act is supposed to give.
Before I reach the main remarks I have to make, let me tell the minister that a great many constituents have telephoned me and talked about the problems they have had with the act and the forms they are required by the minister to complete. Finally, in desperation I have said many times to these people: "Well, if you cannot make it out, do not worry about it. Sign your name to it, put the stuff in an envelope and address it to the minister at the House of Commons-no postage required-because the minister tells me it is pretty simple. So let him look after it".
I am going to address my remarks today to the problems experienced by small businesses with regard to the Income Tax Act and the ancillary forms that must be completed in order to do business in this country in accordance with the act. Small business is pretty important to this country. In the yellow pages of my telephone book, which covers Port Credit, Clarkson and Mississauga, there are pages and pages filled with the addresses of small businesses. Ninety per cent of the ads in these yellow pages are placed by small businesses. Small business represents a tremendous portion of the business activity of the nation.
When the act was first introduced, Mr. Benson introduced what he claimed was the greatest tax system that the world had ever seen. When he announced the tax changes applying to small business, he prefaced them with the following remarks:
This government supports the view that entrepreneurial initiative should be encouraged through the tax system. The Canadian economy depends upon the creative business activity of small, growing businesses.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what have we got? We had a system that was relatively simple: small businesses with earnings under $35,000 paid 20 per cent or 21 per cent corporate tax. We now have a system that is all enmeshed in corporate tax forms, and where at the lower level you pay 25 per cent corporate tax up to the first $50,000 of earnings, providing the cumulative effect of the $50,000 earnings does not exceed $400,000. That is simply to encourage entrepreneurial talent and make you run a small business.
At one time intercorporate dividends were non-taxable. In other words, a dividend paid by a syndicate or by a businessman to the prime company did not carry tax. Under the present system, if this businessman totally controls the subsidiary business, the dividend does not bear tax; but if he does not control it or has a minority interest

in the business, say 49 per cent, that is just tough: the act forces him to take the dividend into the prime company, and it is then passed on either to himself as a shareholder in the prime company or to his family. The complications are totally unreal because companies do have year ends and the dividends must be passed on before the next year end. This is the kind of thing this minister authorizes and this is the kind of problem the businessman faces.
Then, of course, we have the problem of surpluses. We have pre-1972 surpluses, post-1972 surpluses and capital surpluses, and the poor guy in the small business has to figure out when he takes a remittance from his company in the form of a dividend whether he is taking it out of pre-1972 earnings, which he can take out on a flat 15 per cent tax rate, whether it is a regular dividend, or how he can get it out as capital surplus which is not even subject to tax at all. These are the problems to which we must address ourselves.
These are not the only problems. A small businessman is forced to look after a tremendous amount of bookkeeping for this government. These T4 forms are marvelous forms for the average wage earner, but they have to be filled out by every employer. Of course, there are multicarbons; carbon after carbon. They have to go through the Canada Pension Plan and make sure they have deducted, filed and filled in correctly the Canada Pension Plan deductions for their employees. Then, go on in the income tax form to the unemployment insurance portion for their employees, the hospital insurance and other deductions. This does not just involve T4's; it involves T5's, T4A's, T2's and others. These multi-carbon forms have to be filed with the minister, the recipient of income tax, or whoever, before February 28 under penalty, and these forms go on ad nauseam. It is no wonder that businessman after businessman has said to me: Look, if I had to get into it again I would not bother. There is no question about it, businessman after businessman has said this to me and other members, and I bet to the minister himself. They have said they work one-third, one-quarter or half their time looking after the problems of the Minister of National Revenue for free.
Mr. Benson said they were encouraging entrepreneurial talents and initiative through the tax system, but what encouragement is there? Let me talk about the great lie, that situation where we have dividend income and the grossing-up theory. To start off, we have the kind of dividend from the limited company to the individual, and that is all right. However, at the end of the year the corporation which paid the dividend has to produce a T5 slip. On that slip they do not declare what was paid to the individual but one-third more than was paid. Immediately the office is besieged with telephone calls from the shareholders wanting to know what the corporation is trying to do to them. They say they did not receive the money but have received T5 slips indicating a higher dividend. This is the kind of tax problem and form problem this minister has authorized.
The minister said he wanted suggestions. I hope he will sit down, put on his earphone and listen to some suggestions.

Let me return to this whole question of dividends. Under the old system you declared to the recipient the dividend he in fact got. He entered it and took a 20 per cent tax credit. Now, when we have this idea of equity, we gross up and then we take a dividend tax credit. The result to the recipient of the dividend may be that the dividend is tax free in the sense that under the system he gets up to 22 per cent or 23 per cent tax credit, or he may get 17 per cent. The difference is not very much, but most recipients of dividends do not receive that much, yet this whole grossing up and grossing down system is so confusing that the present system is not equity at all. This system authorized by the minister does not represent equity at all, but rather confusion, complexity and ridiculous expense.
Let us now turn to the question of the 25 per cent tax on small business corporations. It used to be about 21 per cent under the old act. The concept of this particular dividend credit system was that a dividend coming from a small business would not be doubly taxed. The effect of the system is to increase that tax to nearly 10 per cent over and above the corporate tax when dividends are taken into account. The complications are even greater when it comes to the situation where a small business, a small company or a proprietor is involved with two or three syndicates or businesses in which he has an interest.
I spoke earlier about passing dividends from one company to another. Small businessmen in particular are forced, because of the nature of the small amount of capital, to go into syndicates or partnerships with other businessmen. Part of the problem created in the act was solved, the Minister of Finance suggested, by his budget. He said that the provisions involving the use of surplus for investment would be allowed, but the minister has not solved this problem of passing on dividends from one company to another. What we must have from the minister is an amendment to the act to allow these changes.
I want now to refer to questions of capital gains as these apply to business in respect of real property, particularly manufacturing, office-oriented or store businesses. Large businesses are usually able to expand because they have the ability to go to the capital market and can work out something in respect of the sale or disposition of property, or the re-use of property for another feature of their activity. The small businessman is not in that fortunate position. If he expands and has to sell his office building, his store or his small factory, he must have the total proceeds of that sale in order to buy his next business, finance his next activity or to complete his expansion. Unfortunately, here the capital gains tax legislation comes into effect because the moment he sells his existing plant and uses the money from that sale to buy another plant he is required to pay a capital gains tax on the first sale.
Income Tax
The problem was apparent in respect of houses of ordinary individuals when the bill was passed and that was taken into account. However, in respect of small businesses the problem remains. The act must be changed so that small business will be allowed to expand by selling one property and using the proceeds to immediately purchase another property without a capital gains tax being imposed on the purchase. No one has a capital gain if he must replace the capital asset instantly for the expansion or continuation of his purposes. No capital gain is made until death do us part. In this respect, small business is seriously penalized in this act and in this form where it is forced to declare the asset, the holdings, the sale of that asset and the tax payable on that asset. The effect on the small business is that its expansion activities are seriously limited.
One of the main problems in connection with this act is the additional accounting costs. My activities prior to coming here were in advising small business firms concerning their taxes and corporate and business problems. I can say that from my personal experience since this act was passed almost every small businessman has faced nearly a 100 per cent increase in his accounting costs. The matter was brought to the attention of small businessmen by A. J. Little, President of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants when he spoke last December in Dartmouth. He said that it would take about two or three times longer for the small businessman to prepare his 1972 income tax return. He said the tax return for small businesses would be vastly more complicated than for the large corporation. He also stated:
"In this respect, we have an upside-down system where the burden of compliance will fall more heavily on individuals and corporations with lower incomes and lower capacity to pay."
I wish now to speak for a moment about a matter which does not appear in the forms except in the corporate sense. This is in connection with the write-off or the depletion or depreciation allowances to be granted to manufacturing companies for equipment bought during 1972, and the confusion that these fast write-off provisions are causing small business. A great number of small businessmen get up in the morning and go out to sell. In the afternoon they are supervising their plant. Many of their employees are both salesmen and machine operators. Some of their employees may be involved in manufacturing today and assembling tomorrow. Many of them are involved in shipping part-time or in delivering something another part of the time. A great deal of their activities involve manufacturing one or two components and importing or buying two or three other components and putting them together. When we come to a separate rate of corporate tax for manufacturing companies, these small corporations who operate in this fashion receive little if any benefit. Indeed, the whole system becomes a tax jungle and an accounting nightmare.

speechtext:
I will tell you about that. When the bill finally passed parliament in 1972 there had been a total of 50 sitting days or about one third the normal time of the session provided for all the legislative steps in respect of this particular bill, so if my friend suggests there was an act of closure I suggest to him he does not know what he is talking about. That is the only really weak remark I have heard him make this afternoon.
I had the privilege to be a member of the opposition in the Ontario legislature for many years. I realize how difficult it is to be a member of an opposition party. I know that sometimes the bottom of the barrel is scraped in order to find criticisms in respect of government policy. This afternoon, however, 1 really think the great Progressive Conservative party made a very serious error in introducing this matter, because up until now members of that party had the whole country terrified about these tax forms. This afternoon we have found they are really not that bad and that the new tax forms contain some redeeming qualities which are acceptable to my friends in the opposition party.
Perhaps I might read from a little pamphlet which, many years ago, was written by a member of this House. Indeed it was written so long ago that perhaps he has forgotten about it. It is entitled "The Role of the Opposition." I remember being handed the pamphlet when I was in Toronto. It says that the opposition of course has a duty to oppose, but it is a duty to oppose constructively, to bring in sound advice for the government. Whether the government accepts that advice is another matter. Probably it will not accept advice from the opposition, but at least the opposition would have done its duty by bringing to the attention of parliament, the government and the

people of Canada what it thinks should be done under certain circumstances.
The income tax forms had to be changed because new tax law was passed by parliament last session. I might remind hon. members that that was not done on the spur of the moment. There are many people in Canada who say tax reform should have taken place years ago, instead of ten years being spent discussing change. Even after the government issued its tax reform paper there was further extensive study for two years. During that time every Canadian had an opportunity to make a contribution to tax reform. Indeed, my hon. friends in the Conservative party who were members of the House of Commons finance committee participated in its deliberations every day and gave their criticism, most of it constructive I thought. To say that they did not have sufficient time and that closure took place is absolutely farcical. Never in our history has more time been devoted, inside or outside parliament, to any legislative matter.
In 1970 the Department of National Revenue taxation branch established its own tax reform task force to engage in basic research so that it would be prepared, as well as possible, to administer the new law. The work of this task force involved development of new systems, technique and procedures, retraining of staff and the creation of a program of assistance to taxpayers. All possible steps were taken to achieve as smooth a transition as possible from the old to the new taxation system. There was neither undue haste in constructing the law nor in its administration. In any jurisdiction where there are such comprehensive changes in the tax law, two or three years are required to iron out all wrinkles, to build up sufficient jurisprudence, etc. There is every indication that the advance planning of the department is resulting in an orderly transition to the new system.
For days, Mr. Speaker, we heard questions put by the hon. member who initiated this debate, complaining that the new tax form is complicated. Quite frankly, just from listening to the Official Opposition, I thought the new tax form was a terrible thing until I studied it over the weekend. The fact is that there are many responsible people in Canada who say it is a very fine form. One can give quotation after quotation from responsible financial people, from television and radio stations and from newspaper people, all to this effect. I give one example. In an editorial on this subject in the Financial Post of March 3, the following appeared:
Speaking at Financial Post's tax strategy conference for the owner/manager, Lyman Maclnnis, a Toronto partner of McDonald, Currie and Co. said:
"The form is not complicated. Furthermore the guide that
accompanies it is a masterpiece. It's the best guide I've seen
anywhere."
I note, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member who moved the motion initiating this debate has left the chamber. This demonstrates his interest in the debate. I say to him and to my hon. friends in the Conservative party that surely they should be able to bring forward a more serious motion, rather than trying to get the people of Canada all worked up and worried about the new tax form. This shows lack of responsibility on their part. They are trying
March 5, 1973

to instil in the people of Canada a lack of confidence in their ability to make out their own tax forms.
The 1972 tax guide consists basically of two parts. The first part is in the colour of the Progressive Conservative party, blue. Maybe that is a mistake. It is the only thing the Conservatives have not criticized. That part is a step by step instruction in completing the form.

speechtext:
My hon. friend, I don't have to have my speeches prepared. If I have any talent at all, it is that I can talk for the next ten or 15 minutes without any notes; but I prefer to be accurate. And I suggest to my hon. friend that when he makes his speech on this topic he should be more accurate than some hon. members on that side of the House.
This blue part is the only section that most taxpayers have to use. The second part contains more detailed information. There has been criticism that too often the guide does not explain fully but refers the taxpayer to his nearest district office. That is done only when a full explanation would require knowledge of the taxpayer's personal situation or when it would be lengthy and complex and of interest to comparatively few people.
I have used these tax offices myself on numerous occasions over the years and I urge people to take advantage of them. The officials are there to help the ordinary taxpayers of Canada. I have had nothing but the greatest courtesy from them; they will bend over backwards to help. The hon. member who moved the motion said that the number of people in the Toronto office had been increased only by 30 to 60. He suggested this meant that one official would have to look after 25,000 inquiries. He should know perfectly well that he was grossly exaggerating beyond even parliamentary bounds. Not all taxpayers go to tax offices. The 60 people in Toronto and the officials in Ottawa, Hamilton and elsewhere do help the taxpayers.
The 1972 guide is new both in design and in substance. Any information required by the majority of taxpayers is in it. The Department of National Revenue taxation branch has been commended by tax authorities in other countries, as well as in Canada, for the simplicity of the guide and its easy to follow instructions. You do not have to take my word for this, Mr. Speaker; just read the newspapers and the editorials. People are beginning to catch on to the fact that even though the form is new, and even though they do not like paying taxes, the Department of National Revenue has done a remarkable job in its first year of dealing with the new form.
When some critics talk about the complexity of the 1972 tax return they are seldom specific about what they mean. Presumably they refer to the guide as well as to the form. I doubt they can offer any evidence that the guide is anything but the best one we have ever had. Most taxpayers will experience no more difficulty in completing the form than they have in recent years.
It would be very nice if the tax form could be as simple as A, B, C. An across the board percentage of all income for tax purposes would require only a few simple forms,
Income Tax
but such a system would be inequitable. Forms are a reflection of the law and of the efforts of the lawmakers to provide an equitable system of taxation. Let us be fair, Mr. Speaker; the tax form is not as complex as many of the critics make it out to be.
This afternoon the mover of the motion gave six reasons why he was introducing his motion. First he said the form was confusing and he gave his opinion on that. This afternoon the minister quoted from speeches and editorials of various people across Canada to show that it is not confusing. It may be confusing in the mind of the hon. member and he is attempting to spread that confusion, for political purposes, all across the country. That is not fair to the people of Canada. Secondly, Mr. Speaker, he said that the grossing up of dividends was illegal and if people had to sign the bottom of these forms it would make them crooks. This suggestion came from the other side of the House even before today.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, not one Progressive Conservative spoke in the last parliament against the grossing up of dividends. Let us suppose for a moment that there might be some substance to the suggestion that the grossing up of dividends is illegal and that the taxpayer did not get the amount that he put down as gross income. Surely it would be equally unbiased to suggest that a person should put in only his net pay instead of his gross pay; in other words, only his take-home pay. Some things have been taken off, such as Canada Pension Plan contributions, income tax deductions, unemployment insurance and hospitalization. In the instance we are discussing, something was taken off as well-the dividend. If the company concerned had not paid corporation taxes there would obviously have been a bigger dividend. For this reason I suggest that if it is right and honest to put down the gross pay, it is also right and honest to put down what the gross dividends would have been had the company concerned not been paying taxes.
There are other provisions in the tax form which my hon. friend suggests are illegal. Three provisions which are reflected in the 1972 tax return but which have not been passed by parliament are the increase from $650 to $1,000 in the old age exemption, the increase from $650 to $1,000 in the disability exemption which is still in existence, and the introduction of the education deduction of $50 a month for full-time attendance at qualifying postsecondary institutions.
Ordinarily, and this was done by the Department of National Revenue, the tax department immediately begins to prepare for tax changes announced in budgets pending parliamentary enactment of legislation; otherwise there would be lengthy delays in their implementation. Enabling legislation is ordinarily passed relatively soon after the budget. In this instance, the government introduced legislation, Bill C-222, to implement the budget provisions but a general election intervened before full consideration and passage of the bill and it died on the order paper in
1972.	The Minister of Finance has clearly indicated that he will introduce legislation as soon as possible in the current session to achieve the same purpose as Bill C-222.

March 5, 1973
Income Tax
Because of time required for design and printing of tax forms, the department was faced with the decision last autumn to include or exclude the aforementioned three items. The decision was taken to include them. Not to include them would have meant that when and if they become law many taxpayers would be forced to file a second return for reassessment. Returns now being filed which are claiming under any of the three provisions are processed to the stage immediately prior to assessment; then they are set aside pending passage of the legislation. When parliament passes the legislation, completion of the assessment can be done quickly and refunds, where they apply, will be mailed with a minimum of delay. Relatively few such returns have been identified so far. Few, if any, taxpayers will suffer any inconvenience if the House deals in the relatively early future with the enabling legislation.
Mr. Speaker, it was with some regret that I saw this motion put before us this afternoon. I must say that I regard it as a strictly political motion. It has done nothing but cause some consternation in the minds of the public. It has not always been my practice to congratulate ministers, but in this instance I think the minister has done an outstanding job.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course, if there had not been the resolution we would not have been treated to the speech by the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher). I am glad he likes the blue forms. If they are so simple, I wonder why the government has seen fit to spend such an inordinate amount of money on the Fred Davis advertisements. One of my constituents was so upset by the "world's best income tax forms" that she bundled them all up and sent them to Fred Davis because she was sure he would fix them up for her. I am informed that Fred Davis himself gave up attempts to deal with his income tax returns and sent the forms to his accountant.
I want to take the few minutes that are allocated to me, Mr. Speaker, to discuss one aspect of income tax, that is, the right of our citizens to privacy. I think perhaps this aspect has been overlooked by all but a couple of editorialists. I do not purport to have a series of endorsations of

my position that will take up the rest of my time, but I do seriously think that matters of privacy and mutual trust are questions that this parliament should be concerned about.
The whole structure of income tax collection in Canada has been based on mutual trust. The Department of National Revenue relies on the taxpayer to make an honest statement of his income, and the taxpayer relies on the department to keep secret the information about his affairs except in tax evasion proceedings. To the question, "Will the tax man tell?" the answer seems to be that he will, depending on who asks and for what purpose. There is a frighteningly long list of officials, authorized persons and others who have some claim to the production of income tax data. I think this is an area that should be of general concern to parliament and to the taxpayers of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INCOME TAX-SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FILING FORMS AND LEGALIZATION OF 1972 STRUCTURE AND FORMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-INCOME TAX-SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF TIME FOR FILING FORMS AND LEGALIZATION OF 1972 STRUCTURE AND FORMS
speechtext:
Although officials or authorized persons may not intentionally communicate income tax information to anybody except those persons specified by law in prescribed circumstances, the list of persons to whom communication of some kind is permitted turns out to be fairly long. For instance, there are "other officials and authorized persons", there are "provincial governments", there are "persons otherwise legally entitled", which I suggest might include the chief statistician of Canada, certain foreign governments, the trustee in bankruptcy, the liquidator, the courts in certain circumstances, royal commissions investigating tax matters, the attorney general, the taxpayer who provided the information in the first place and his legal agent or representative.
An official or authorized person can be compelled to reveal income tax information in criminal proceedings under any federal law, not only in tax fraud cases. I think this is a matter of some surprise to people. We usually think of income tax forms as being sacrosanct. The law uses the expression "may", but I suggest that anybody who can show that he is entitled to income tax information under the loose wording of the act can probably compel disclosure.
The definition of "official" is particularly broad. The Income Tax Act provides that an official is any person employed in, or occupying a position of responsibility in the service of Her Majesty, or any person formerly so employed or formerly occupying a position therein. That definition seems to include all ministers, deputy ministers and senior civil servants and does not even exclude former ministers or former civil servants.
An official in the course of his duties investigating the affairs of a taxpayer would not be contravening section 241(1), the basic secrecy section, if he communicated information to a former high civil servant currently in the business world. It may be that I am drawing a wide bow here; I am doing this to emphasize the dangers. According to the present act, it is possible for a former official to be in possession of information regarding a taxpayer under investigation.
March 5, 1973

When an income tax return is produced in open court, there is nothing in the act to prevent the judge quoting from the form in full, not only facts about income but all the details of dependents, medical expenses and charitable donations. There is nothing to prevent the party to the legal dispute who has obtained the income tax return from communicating its contents in full to anybody he chooses. There is not even anything to prevent persons who happen to wander into the courtroom that day from finding out every detail contained in the tax return and communicating that information to others; yet the person whose income tax return is so disclosed might very well be acquitted.
Canadians, I think, have been led to believe that their income tax returns are as secret as their census returns or their ballots. Yet I suggest very seriously that recent events cast doubt on this assumption. A recent case has shaken that sssumption and revealed that legal protection for the confidentiality of tax returns is far from complete.
Richard Green, LL.M., of Queen's University, who now is a research associate at the Canadian Tax Foundation in Toronto, published a study in the January issue of the Canadian Tax Journal in which he concludes that the present legal position of income tax returns is "illogical and can lead to injustice." Mr. Green points specifically to the wording of the Income Tax Act which according to him shows a bias in favour of the taxpayer's privacy, but once legal proceedings begin, the returns and the documents from which they are compiled can be introduced in evidence. The balance swings from the privacy of the individual to the administration of justice. Mr. Green's summary of the present legal position regarding income tax confidentiality indicates that the effect of wording which sounds as if it is providing broad protection of privacy is considerably whittled away by the exceptions contained in section 241(8) (9) and (10) and by court proceedings.
As it is nearly six o'clock, I should like to make one or two suggestions. One of them would interest the hon. member for Bruce, that hon. member who is so upset about attendance but who has left the chamber. The first suggestion comes from Mr. I. H. Asper, a Winnipeg lawyer and leader of the Manitoba Liberal party. Understandably, he finds the form not to his liking. Mr. Asper feels that the commitment of the government to protect the secrecy of taxpayers should be maintained. He wants to make sure that that principle will not be breached. Mr. Asper feels that an assurance to this effect ought to be repeated. I am sure he hopes that the assurance will come from the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury).
The former minister of national revenue has said only that the policy of the Department of National Revenue is to do only what is permitted under section 241 of the Income Tax Act. Regrettably, that section in its wording is almost as vague as the minister was, enough so to make one wonder if Canada's entire system of income tax is indeed in peril. If Canada's system of self-reporting income tax is to be regarded as a mutual trust, it should be publicly declared as such by the government.
Second, I do not think there is room for a nebulous category of persons "otherwise legally entitled". The taxpayer should know precisely who has access to his income
Income Tax
tax return and in what situations. Third, only the relevant part of an income tax return, if produced in court, should become part of the public record. One of the reasons for the present legal situation is the breakdown of Crown privilege in relation to income tax returns as a class of documents. If I may interpolate, the doctrine of Crown privilege is a legal doctrine which gives a minister of the Crown the right to withhold documents on the ground that their publication would be contrary to the public interest. The courts have generally refused to accept the idea that all income tax returns are in a class of documents of this kind. Judges have asserted their right to examine the individual tax returns involved to see whether the revenue minister is right in claiming that the public interest would be damaged by their publication.
Lastly, the assistant deputy attorney general said that the justice department is entitled to use information given to the income tax department in cases in which the good of public administration and the administration of justice are concerned. I suggest, with respect, that as matters stand, the information provided on our income tax forms could wind up being widely discussed. I conclude by reading an excerpt from an editorial that appeared in the Financial Times on January 15 of this year. It reads in part:
What is needed is a simple prohibition preventing the use of income tax information for anything but the collection of the tax itself and the prosecution of the taxpayer for having falsified his return.
I suggest that what the public expects is a statement to the effect that that is the law. I would be obliged if, during the course of this debate, someone speaking on behalf of the Minister of National Revenue would clarify the record and make that assertion in parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the motion before the House to try to explain as simply as I can the method of determining the amount of deduction from tax in respect of dividends, referred to as the dividend tax credit. This method for 1972 requires that an individual include in income an amount that is in addition to the amount of dividends he actually receives, but it should be noted that the individual may then deduct from his federal tax, not from his income, an amount equal to 20 per cent of the total amount he has added to his income on account of the dividends. Thus, the fact that an amount in addition to the dividend must be included in income increases the amount that may be deducted from an individual's tax.

March 5, 1973
Income Tax
The effect of the dividend tax credit is to substantially lower the amount of tax payable on a dividend. For example, if an individual had $7,000 of taxable income before counting his dividend, and he received a dividend of $300, the federal tax on the dividend, if there were no dividend tax credit, would be 25 per cent of $300 which is $75. Under the tax credit arrangement in effect for 1972 he would include $400 in income on account of the dividend. The tax on this would be 25 per cent, which is $100, but his dividend tax credit deductible from tax would be 20 per cent of $400, which is $80, and this would wipe out a large part of the tax payable in respect of his dividend.
Some taxpayers express concern that the additional amount that must be included in income in respect of a dividend will place them in a higher tax bracket. This is a misunderstanding. A progressive income tax system, such as that in Canada, uses a graduated rate schedule which imposes an increased rate of tax upon each additional bracket of income. As a result of this system, the additional amount included in income in respect of a dividend may, in some cases, fall into a higher bracket and be subject to a higher marginal or top rate than the dollars received before including this income, but additional income does not affect the rate of tax on all the income of a taxpayer. To illustrate, if a taxpayer had exactly $2,000 of taxable income, which means income after all exemptions and deductions, the rate schedule for 1972 would impose a federal tax of $365 on that amount. This is about 18 per cent of $2,000. Each additional dollar of income over the $2,000, up to $3,000, would be taxed at 20 per cent. This is a higher rate than the tax on the first $2,000, but these additional dollars of taxable income would not affect the amount of tax on the $2,000. As explained before, the additional amount added to income in respect of the dividend increases the amount of the dividend tax credit which is a deduction from tax.
Most Canadians agree that it is desirable that Canadians be encouraged to invest in shares of Canadian companies. This is one of the main reasons why the tax law provides a credit against tax in respect of dividends from Canadian corporations. The change in the method of computing this credit introduced for 1972 made the credit more valuable to those with low incomes than to those with high incomes.
Some taxpayers have asked why a change was made from the previous method of computing the dividend tax credit and why it should be necessary to increase the actual dividend by one-third to arrive at the figure shown in box B on the T-5 slips, called "Taxable amount". This procedure, sometimes called grossing up, has two effects. First, by increasing the amount of the dividend, thereby increasing the shareholder's income and the size of his credit, the situation that would have existed had not the corporate profits been taxed in the hands of the corporations is more closely approximated. Second, the grossing-up of the dividend is equivalent to providing a larger credit and making the amount of the credit taxable. As a result, the dividend tax credit tends to be more beneficial to the lower income taxpayers than to those with higher incomes.
This may be a brief explanation, Mr. Speaker, but it shows that this method of calculating the credit is fair and, I think, practical in this situation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to rise in this House to discuss such a troublesome matter to the people of Canada as the new tax forms with which a great many Canadians will have to cope this year. They are confusing. No amount of public relations or speech-making in this House will resolve that confusion. I can sympathize with the people who prepared the forms, the schedules and the brochure because obviously one of the basic reasons the form is confusing is that the law which was established in this House is indeed complicated. It makes it very difficult to prepare a form which is easy to follow when the law is obtuse and pretty well concealed from even the bulk of the tax authorities in this country.
The form is mammoth compared with last year's form. This was demonstrated by one of my friends on this side of the House in the photograph referred to earlier by the minister. The guide, perhaps somewhat more psychedelic than it was before, does not have the appearance of any confusion. In fact, it appears quite orderly on the surface. Indeed, some aspects of it are very easy to understand. I wish to read into the record one or two excerpts which I think are meritorious on the part of the people who drafted the guide. One of the most striking is the first paragraph in this booklet:
Stripped of all its mystery, a tax form is simply a piece of paper on which you do four basic things:
(1)	identify yourself.
(2)	lsit your income.
(3)	reduce your income by subtracting allowable deductions.
(4)	calculate your tax.
That is a masterful touch on the part of the draftsman. Indeed, if that were all there were to preparing the income tax return which this year the government has placed before the people of Canada, there would be no trouble at all in preparing it. What else do we find in the little book? The answer is the blue pages. These are prepared, it says, for almost all taxpayers. But if we follow the blue pages carefully, we find there is no mention anywhere of listed property. It would seem that the great mass of the taxpayers who are expected to fill out these forms do not possess any property which falls into this category. The taxpayer who this year will be able to follow these blue pages is the taxpayer who last year used the simple T-l form, the taxpayer who has no income other than his earnings from employment, the taxpayer who has no savings, the taxpayer who owns no chattels worth any significant amount of money-or, if he does, he is not dealing in them because certainly values do not need to be very extraordinary before the blue pages no longer apply.
I have now found the quotation I was looking for in this section. It reads:
While this section will probably not be needed by most people-
The reference is to income from other sources. Mr. Speaker, there are few people who do not derive income from some other sources. This, it seems to me, portrays

March 5, 1973

the attitude of the government, one which will come to fruition in the future when most people will not even be able to invest in a Canada savings bond by way of saving for their old age. Obviously, if they have such an investment they will not be able to fill out the form on the basis of this section. This form is designed for the Canadian taxpayer of the future. It is designed for the poor taxpayer of the future, perhaps even in 1973 when the citizen cannot save sufficient money from which to make investments, buy a cottage for which he might incur a tax liability or acquire a work of art worth more than $1,000.
Then we turn to the aspect of the guide dealing with capital gains. A capital gains tax is one which the great majority of Canadians consider to be applicable only to the wealthy, to those born with a silver spoon in their mouth. But one need not read for very long in the guide before determining that there are not many Canadians who will escape the penalties contained in these provisions affecting capital gains. I want to read one excerpt from that section in the guide which has gone to the other extreme. The compiler of this guide started out in good faith, but by page 27 he is bogging down a bit. It reads:
To compute a capital gain or loss on an asset acquired before 1972, three figures are required:
-the actual cost -the valuation day value
-the proceeds of disposition as described above.
(Note that adjustments to the cost base may change the proceeds
of disposition for this purpose.)
The median of these three figures-
I always understood that the median was half way between two points, and thus one could not have a median somewhere between three figures. It may be I am lacking in appreciation of the niceties of the language and do not understand what it means, but I suggest there are a great many taxpayers who will not be able to understand this, either. It continues:
-that is, the figure which is neither the highest nor the lowest, is the base upon which the capital gain or loss is computed, subject to the election explained below. Where two or more of these three figures are in the same amount, that amount will be the median. This median figure is deemed to be the adjusted cost of the asset and is the amount to be entered in column 2 of schedule 2, provided that there are no adjustments as outlined in item 58. If there are adjustments, contact your district taxation office.
