speechtext:
At about the time I got to that line I had already decided I would rush to my accountant as soon as I had dug up all the information necessary to determine exactly what had to be done.
Item 68 in the guide talks about valuation day. Valuation day is a concept which will soon come home to Canadian taxpayers. I suggest that the item in the guide constitutes a trap, especially for the taxpayer who does not take the precaution to consult someone who is knowledgeable about the provisions of the new act.
Today we have heard members on the other side encouraging taxpayers to file tax returns this year without consulting anyone with special knowledge of the tax situation. This might be because there are so few people
Income Tax
who thoroughly understand the legislation: witness the statement by Mr. Thorson, as I understand it, that there were only half a dozen such people in the world, of whom he was one and the other five were in his department. How is a person to get fair treatment when it comes to the disposal of his assets if he starts off without receiving proper advice from a tax expert on whether to make an election to use valuation day values or values on acquisition?
Many taxpayers will make a mistake; they will do the wrong thing, and in years to come they will incur a severe penalty. It may be said that the tax law applies to everyone else in the same way it applies to them, but the initial error might have been made simply because they were not accustomed to receiving expert advice when preparing their tax forms. This in itself is a good reason for allowing an extension of time during which taxpayers would have an opportunity to receive professional advice.
Another curious thing about this tax form is that there is no provision for deducting losses in most cases of change in capital value. The only thing the government seems to be concerned with are capital gains. Those who lose go pretty much unrewarded or without much of a deduction.
The detailed information that is required to complete the income tax return is, I suggest to the House, a most serious invasion of privacy. The information that is required in terms of filing valuation day reports calls for the most soul searching determination of every asset that a family owns that might possibly have some value, particularly those that might have a value of over $1,000 in terms of 1972 dollars, which will be worth heaven knows what in ten years' time.
Eventually this will surely mean the declaration of every piece of jewellery and every jewel that is an heirloom in the family, every jewel of value that is passed from mother to daughter. Antique furniture that may have acquired value over the years is another item. It is easy to cite examples of furnishings that will be worth over $1,000 and which have been passed down from generation to generation. Perhaps paintings are an even better example. I suggest this constitutes a very substantial tax by virtue of the continuing inflation that this country has experienced during the past few years. At the current rate, I suggest that when we are compiling an inventory of our personal assets we might be very wise to keep the receipts for underwear that we have bought; with inflation going the way it is, that might end up worth over $1,000 too.
I want to consider for a moment the impact that these forms, and perhaps the forms that will be incorporating the provisions of the 1972 budget resolutions, will have on manufacturing industries. Again the taxpayer, particularly the small businessman, is going to be faced with a substantial tax, not just because of the inflationary aspect of capital gains that I mentioned a moment ago but because small businesses will be required to retain tax consultants to an extent they never have before. In a lot of cases, instead of a business having a part-time accountant or accounts kept by the proprietor himself, a full-time

Income Tax
accountant will be needed to keep track of all capital transactions, as well as revenue and expenditure incurred in the normal course of business. This will mean an additional tax in the form of money expended on appraisal fees to defend the company against any tax levy that the department may seek to impose upon them in the future.
Furthermore, there is the uncertainty of never knowing whether a valuation day report will be acceptable to the department. If it is overruled, a businessman may then require legal advice, again involving him in further expense which could be considered akin to a legal fees tax. Legal experts would need to be employed to argue a case before the Tax Appeal Board. Then, again, any attempt to pass on a business that is not a family farm to members of one's family faces another tax.
All these things result from the effect of this legislation upon small business. By "small business" I speak of the businessman who does business in my constituency of South Western Nova where there are many fish plants, fishermen who own their own boats, and lumber mills. These people do a volume of business of perhaps $250,000 a year and employ 15 to 20 persons. What will be the impact upon those persons when they attempt to determine the income they derive from manufacturing and processing and other facets of their business? For example, take the case of the owner of a fish plant who may also be a boat owner, a fish buyer who may be in the business of filleting fresh fish and shipping them to market as they are, a man who is in the business of freezing and packaging, or a person who is in the business of fish sales and brokerage. Freezing and packaging apparently come under the manufacturing or processing provisions of the legislation. This kind of businessman will not reap any of the benefits of the legislation; rather, it will be a liability to him.
As I say, I represent a rural riding, one with many small businesses and old people. My riding has perhaps a higher percentage of older people than other ridings in Canada, and some aspects of these new forms are particularly troublesome to the elderly. The advertising program that was instituted by the government to familiarize Canadians with the forms and to convince them that it was easy to fill them out did not really cover local areas where the great proportion of the population do not take the large dailies but read the weeklies. The government did not see fit, at least initially, to advertise in the weeklies; as a result, people in the rural areas were not made aware of how "easy to understand" these forms are. As a result, they were a month or two behind, psychologically speaking, in preparing themselves for the insurmountable task of filing their 1972 income tax return.
Most federal and private tax consulting offices, as I understand it, have been forced to extend their office hours in order to cope with the increased demands that are being made upon them. I understand a great many of them are keeping their offices open until nine o'clock and that the government has experienced a similar phenomenon as far as their own information facilities for taxpayers are concerned. At the same time, tax consultants and accountants have naturally found it necessary to increase their fees since the time consumed in preparing these

March 5, 1973
returns has increased. Thus, the cost of retaining an accountant has increased this year.
As I mentioned earlier, when the associate deputy minister of justice was asked about this Income Tax Act while speaking to the Tax Foundation, he stated that only six people fully understood the act; they were himself and five of his employees.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to bring a few things to the attention of the minister and the House. I wrote to the minister some time ago because of a problem which had been brought to my attention by an accountant in my area. The minister was good enough to reply. In addition, he sent me a short note on February 26 in which he said that during the tax return filing period, if I had developed some ideas or had received opinions from constituents about tax forms, and so on, I might be kind enough to bring them forward. This evening I should like to bring to the attention of the minister and the House several matters that have been brought to my attention. He may agree that some of them require correction or he may say that there really is not a problem. All I can do is bring these problems to the attention of the minister.
I have an accountant friend who does what I need to be done in filing a return. He said to me as far back as last fall that accountants were going to have difficulty with the new provisions. Some of the things which have come to my attention indicate that these difficulties have occurred. I would refer to a letter I received from an accountant. I sent this to the minister and asked for a reply and he was good enough to provide one. This accountant pointed out that there was real confusion in regard to capital gains tax as it applied to farmers claiming under part 11 as against part 17. Under part 11, the recovery provisions provided prior to 1972 would work
March 5, 1973

out all right but under part 17 they would not. The accountant who wrote to me detailed this at some length.
The minister replied that this would be corrected to some extent, or perhaps altogether, by the ways and means motions that might come in February, 1973. This may be so, and probably is. But what puzzles me is why on earth the taxation proposal for the farm business did not simply leave things on a straight cash reporting basis in simple and easy terms, so returns could be filed by farmers and the people who often do filing in rural communities and prepare estimates of farmers' income returns. If this is a provision in respect of which a chartered accountant finds it necessary to point out the difficulties which exist, and asks me to do what I can to have them clarified, then those who drafted these provisions in the first place did not do their job. Indeed, there are a number of areas in which these gentlemen did not do their job.
Let me point out one area in respect of cattle herds and the farmer and rancher who make their living, or part of it, from raising cattle. When this legislation was going through the House we on this side pleaded with the government to leave the basic herd concept alone, but they would not do that. They wiped out the basic herd concept and had to come back with another proposal in this budget which I understand, and I can be corrected, means that the farmer can take a build-up into inventory at some point of time and spread it over a period of years. Why adopt this involved method of doing things as against a simple concept which existed and worked? I do not know the answer.
Anyone who has anything to do with income tax knows that if you are going to dispose of a cattle herd, take it into inventory and spread it over a number of years, thereby saving yourself income tax in one particular year, you must plan to do that some time ahead. If a farmer has not received the advice of an income tax consultant that he is able to do this and save himself money, he will not know this provision is available to him and will not take advantage of it. He will end up paying more taxes than he should.
There were two courses open to the government, either to retain the basic herd concept or adopt another simple method to allow a farmer or a rancher to set up his cattle herd as a depreciable asset, just as you might with machine tools in a factory or, indeed, machinery on the farm.

Let me deal briefly with the capital gains proposal, that is, to set aside the tax in the case where a farm stays in the family on the death of the father. Why was this provision restricted to the time of death? Most people are aware that many farms are transferred during the lifetime of the

farmer. Why not make this applicable during his lifetime, particularly if the objective is to facilitate the transfer without hardship to the family and to maintain a farm within the family? Mr. Speaker, having examined the first motion which the opposition had the opportunity to introduce, I am surprised to see that they had nothing to find fault with, except the income tax forms which apparently are complex and illegal. Evidently, I cannot discuss whether they are illegal or not because I do not think that I have the necessary qualifications to do so since I am not a lawyer. However, I am quite surprised that they lay no other blame upon the government.
We are told that the income tax forms are confusing and that we must speed up the payment of income tax refunds to over 6 million taxpayers. Therefore, I am pleased to note that the opposition has nothing else to hold against us.
As for this year's income tax returns, I think they can be explained easily. People with lesser education than the hon. member for York Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) or others can complete the form themselves without being helped by an accountant or a lawyer. I was able to experience it myself for people asked me how was the form as compared with last year's and they realized that it is much simpler because in 1971 and before, income tax returns varied with income. There were then the T-l Short, and the T-l General for those in business or whose income was over a specified maximum.
And if my memory serves me right, the maximum was then $8,000. As for the 1971 guide, I suggest that it was much more complicated than that for the present year, all

the more so since it only applied to those who had to fill a T1 short form.
Moreover, it has to be said that the tax table for 1971 and the previous years was made for incomes up to $8,000, which means that many taxpayers whose income was over $8,000 necessarily had to make what was called a detailed tax calculation on a form which was attached to the T-l General Form. As far as the T-l short from is concerned, this calculation could not be done because this form only applied to people whose income was $8,000 or less.
This year, the 1972 tax table enables those who have an income of $12,000 to know what amount of tax they have to pay without making a detailed calculation, and I suggest that this is a definite improvement.
I would like to refer as well to an article published in Le Soleil of February 3, 1973, and written by Monique Payeur. I quote:
In order to have a more equitable tax system,-
And I believe that our tax system is more equitable than it has ever been, after ten years of study.
-tile federal government has made a complete review of its top legislation and introduces for 1972 a standard tax form for everybody-
In 1972, for instance, the federal government published eleven small booklets in the series "Tax Reform", dealing with specific points of the new tax policy, like child care expenses, travel expenses, capital gains, basic herds, etc.
Therefore, the people who must pay taxes have already received from the Department of National Revenue booklets explaining how to make this calculation, since this is a new act developped as a result of studies carried out by the House. We received the Carter report and, later on, we studied the white paper on the tax reform for a year and a half to two years. This was followed by the introduction of a bill which represented a rather drastic tax reform, needless to say, to help more those who earned less because they are overtaxed compared with other taxpayers.
When the tax reform was studied by this House, several arguments were invoked, for an against, of course, but it was passed and later on, as I have already mentioned, the Department of National Revenue sent out brochures to the people explaining the new deductions to which they were entitled and also the whys and wherefores of those deductions.
I fail to see any problem, all the more so considering the fact that an income tax act, in as complex a business world as ours, cannot be simple. To my mind, the department managed to produce a fairly simple form, in view of course of the complexity of the act.
This act was not necessarily prepared by the Liberal party; it was prepared while the Liberal party was in power, as it has been for many years, and will be for many years to come. The Liberal party called on specialists. Indeed, within the Department of National Revenue, there is an advisory committee made up of legal advisers, specialists in the field of taxation and accountants. These people got together and assisted department officials in preparing the simplest form possible.
And the one that we are considering and for whose defects we are condemned by its opponents is not merely

a product of members of the Liberal party or officials of the Income tax Division, but also that of people from the private sector, specialists in this field, who have worked hard trying to draft a personal income tax form which would make it easier for the individual to complete his income tax return and which would at the same time comply with the provisions of the new Income Tax Act which, obviously, is rather complex because in a modern and complex world it is very hard to draft a very simple law.
However, they did achieve something quite simple to prepare, covering a maximum of four pages. First of all, identification of the individual involved, which poses no problems. For those who have incomes other than remuneration for their employment, something very useful has been prepared, the appendixes.
Formerly, there were no schedules. What happened was that people had to prepare their own for submission to the tax bureau. Now, these schedules are supplied.
Schedule 1 includes detailed calculation of taxes applying only to those having incomes of $12,000 and over, thus probably eliminating at least half of taxpayers who do not have to do anything about schedule I.
Schedule 2 concerns statement of capital dispositions. Of course, formerly when sales of capital goods had been carried out, an accountant had to be hired to make out such a document for the civil servant checking this formula, with details of the sale compared with the cost, and so on.
What has been added is the provision concerning capital gains and losses. Now, one of those who spoke before me suggested that the guide contained nothing about capital losses. Well I found out that it does contain something. The government cannot collect from Canadian taxpayers more than they must pay, but really what all Canadians must pay according to the law.
And I am surprised that the hon. member for York-Simcoe, who submitted that motion, has not shown more interest in it; because after he had presented it this afternoon, he disappeared and has not been seen since.
This simply proves the weakness of the Progressive Conservatives' motion. In my opinion, that motion does not make any sense.
Furthermore, schedule 3 deals with medical expenses and charitable donations. But it's not everyone who has to report any for deduction purposes, and the government has added a schedule for them to give the details of the receipts they have in their possession, so that they can claim that deduction.
The income tax return contains a section to make a statement of investment income. Now, in the 1971 form, the reporting of investment income was mentioned, but very briefly, so that many people complained that there was not enough space to report that income properly. Of course for those who make investments, a schedule has been added this year. Once again, I fail to see the difficulty in referring to this annex.
Schedule 5 deals with child care expenses. Of course we had to include child care expenses in the 1972 returns,
Income Tax
because they are something new. They were brought in by the Liberal party and the taxpayers have welcomed them. If they were to profit from their deductions, we obviously had to include an annex for people to note the details of their expenditure in this field.
Schedule 6 deals with additional personal exemptions. Those who have difficulties with their married persons' exemptions and wish to be taxed otherwise than as persons married to a legitimate spouse, will require a special form for additional information so that they can qualify for married status.
Schedule 7 deals with real estate rentals. A good many Canadians are now property owners, we are pleased to see, and receive a small income from this. Rather than force them to consult an accountant and spend money to have a statement of their real estate income and expenditure drawn up, we printed an annex, which will obviously be of help to them.
For those who receive other income, such as sales commission, we added another annex, 9, which is a statement of income and expenses. Here again, this spares the taxpayers the expense of professional advice in making out his return.
A look at the guide, about which a member was making such a fuss just now, shows that it is very clear. It sets up six steps in making out one's return. The first is explained under the heading of "Getting ready", and is obviously that of getting together the papers needed to make out the return. I do think that there are no special difficulties on that.
Step two under the heading "Identifying yourself" is to say who you are. There is no problem on that either, I believe.
Step three, under the heading "Listing your income" is to indicate the income and then some information is given on taxable and non taxable income. A little further, the guide lists especially the income that does not necessarily need to be declared.
Step four, under the heading "Claiming your deductions", deals with allowable deductions. It is quite clear: there are the "Canada Pension Plan contributions." There is no problem on that either. As for contributions to a "Registered Pension Plan", people were previously entitled to only $1,500; the Liberal party, in its tax reform, has granted them an exemption of $2,500. In my opinion, all Canadians are very pleased about it.

In the early fifties the preparation of these tax returns was a relatively simple matter; however, as years went by it became more and more complicated. Ministerial decisions, regulations and amendments to the act-

speechtext:
The public, the accountants and the tax lawyers were flattered. At long last, here was a man who was going to make sense out of our tax system. We all waited with anticipation. Here was a man who was going to give us a new Income Tax Act, one that could be understood
March 5, 1973

and one that would replace the antiquated patchwork act passed, I believe, in 1918 or 1919. Hon. Edgar Benson listened in two official languages but he answered us in a language more incomprehensible than that which might have been used by a visitor from outer space.
I had occasion in November, 1971, to attend the Canadian Tax Foundation seminar in Vancouver. In attendance at that meeting were leading tax experts from all over Canada, men who specialize in income tax, men who had spent upwards of nine months studying the then proposed tax act which was subsequently passed, of course, in December of that year. These men were united in stating that a great many of the sections of the act were completely unintelligible to most experts unless they could understand the operation of a computer and calculate algebraic formulas backwards. This is the act upon which our income tax return is now based, Mr. Speaker, an act that has required the department to spend, I do not know how many hundreds of thousands of dollars on explanatory booklets and interpretation bulletins some of which themselves require interpretation.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) indicated that the new income tax form is not complicated. He even hired a well known television personality to advertise the fact that the return, close up, is easier than it looks. Obviously, hon. members on the other side of the House who have spoken, including the hon. member who spoke prior to me, should themselves appear on television instead of spending money on a television personality. We should put those tax experts on the air and save hundreds of thousands of dollars. I think the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc) hit the nail on the head when he said that the tax form is simple in relation to the complexity of the legislation. I think that is absolutely correct. The legislation is complicated, and the tax return must be complicated.
It may be that the physical act of completing the return is not difficult once the information has been gathered together, but it is essential that the taxpayer compile the necessary information. In order to do so, he must have knowledge of the act and of the law. It must not just be cursory, otherwise he will find himself in difficulties with the assessor and the department and subject to penalties which in some cases are much more severe than penalties imposed under the Criminal Code. But at least under the Criminal Code one can get a conditional discharge.
Should a taxpayer be required to spend hours, or even days studying interpretation bulletins and tax guides in order to complete a tax return or, alternatively, should he have to spend money to retain the services of a tax expert or accountant in order to complete a return? The majority of taxpayers just cannot afford the luxury. They require those dollars to help them cope with the spiralling cost of living which continues to plague us. It may be suggested by the government that if a taxpayer reads and studies "Your Guide to the 1972 Income Tax Return" and/or the "1972 Farmers' and Fishermen's Tax Guide", the taxpayer can complete his own return. That may be so if the taxpayer is a scholarly type, has a basic understanding of the law and has spent weeks or even months studying it: under those conditions, perhaps he can fill out the return. However, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that unless a farmer
Income Tax
taxpayer who is preparing his own T1 general form has a good understanding of capital cost allowances and has read the "1972 Farmers' and Fishermen's Tax Guide" with a good deal of care, he could easily come to the conclusion that he must depreciate all assets under part II of the regulations rather than under part 17, regardless of when he acquired them. Once he converted, the decision would be irreversible.
What about capital gains? The hon. member for Laurier looked over the income tax return and made light of the difficulties. He suggested that there is no problem in filling it out. The income tax return, if the taxpayer disposes of some capital assets, requires an election to be made. I ask, how can an individual taxpayer make an election under section 26(7) of the Income Tax Application Rules, 1971, unless he knows what the ramifications are? Once he makes that election which is set out at the bottom of the second page of the return, he is bound by it for the rest of his life, and his estate after him is bound by that election.
There is a very important principle which says that no man should have to pay a tax which he cannot reasonably be expected to understand. The government seems to have forgotten that principle, Mr. Speaker. There are new complications to do with partnerships. Professional people who are on a cash basis, or were on a cash basis previously, will encounter many problems. The matter of professional partnerships is especially complicated.
As there are a large number of uncertainties regarding the law of partnership and as much complexity is involved in the calculations, much additional time will be required to be spent by accountants in preparing returns. I am advised by chartered accountants and by tax consultants in my constituency that all returns this year will require a much longer time for completion than previous returns did, partly because of the queries raised by taxpayers and partly because the election I mentioned must be considered and studied where capital gains are involved. I do not envy the chartered accountant who is called on for advice with respect to an election to do with capital gains. In many cases he might be just as well off if he were to make his decision after gazing into a crystal ball.
I am also advised that many accountants feel that because of the additional time required to complete returns they will encounter difficulty in meeting the April 30 deadline. For that reason they are accepting very few new clients. An extension of one month in the filing date is essential if taxpayers are to be given the opportunity of obtaining professional advice and services. I believe, Mr. Speaker, although I have been unable to substantiate my assertion, that an extension of time was granted to farmers in 1950 for the filing of 1949 returns. I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to an extension this year.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, let me say that a tax system which is so complicated that it cannot be understood by the individual taxpayer without professional advice, and which requires a taxpayer to pay a government department a fee in order that he may obtain a decision regarding the interpretation of the act, is totally unacceptable.

March 5, 1973
Income Tax

It is the one place where almost every citizen in the community comes in contact with the government. Similarly, this is the one area where I think it is the compelling duty of the government to make sure a person understands the relationship that exists between the citizen and his government.

When I finish my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will accept the question, if I may. There are a few remarks I wish to make. To set my remarks in perspective, may I be permitted to outline the chronology which led to our present incredible situation. We taxpayers are being required to sign income tax returns which are to include particulars of income and exemptions that as yet have no basis in law. There is a dilemma for you.
(Mr. Cafik.)
March 5, 1973
As to the chronology, the budget address of May, 1972, contained tax cuts and other exemptions for many classes of Canadian taxpayers. However, before these provisions could be considered by parliament, the government adjourned the House on July 7. Then the House next sat in special session on August 31 and September 1 to deal with the B.C. longshoremen's strike. After that the House was dissolved for the general election of October 30, with the budget proposals still not discussed.
The House did not meet again until January 4. As a result, due to the government's inaction, millions of taxpayers have been placed in a state of confusion and uncertainty, not to mention-as matters stand at this moment-if they are filling in their income tax forms, in illegality. To backtrack a bit, following the presentation of May, 1972, the Liberals refrained from introducing their budget bills for 34 sitting days after the budget address. It was not until June 26, 1972, in fact that the finance minister tabled bills to amend the Income Tax Act, the Excise Tax Act and the Customs Tariff. The Canadian public, therefore, had some cause to wonder why that delay was necessary in tabling these bills. Whatever the reasons, and these we can only suspect, the upshot was that there was not time to debate these bills before parliament was adjourned, eight sitting days later. With no move made to debate these bills during the emergency session, the bills lapsed.
The government could have remedied the situation by calling parliament shortly after the election, but for reasons of its own it did not. The fact that no action was taken on these bills meant that measures of assistance to both individual and corporate taxpayers were not acted upon. There is no excuse that I can see for the government having deferred implementation of these budget proposals in this manner. The necessary bills could have been introduced, as is normally the case, immediately after the budget speech. Parliament need not have been dissolved before they were acted upon or, at the very least, the government could have called the session before the new year to deal with them.
Instead, the government chose to ignore the bills and to introduce another budget in which some of the more controversial measures of the May 8 budget were omitted, for overt reasons of political expediency. The only part of the budget to be enacted were non-budgetary items referring to old age security pensions, exemptions and veterans benefits-what can be called the vote catching items: the nitty-gritty's and the difficult bits were put aside.
Are we going to be faced with deadlines as we so often have in the past, hours of time requiring measures to be passed so that the government can get these returns in on April 30 as required? Would it not have been possible to begin the first session of the twenty-ninth parliament in December, breaking for the Christmas recess, rather than waiting until January? This obviously reveals the government's set of priorities, where political concerns rate higher than do human considerations.
What is the outcome of these tactics? As of now we are faced with a series of illegalities. The government's handling of the whole income tax issue does not conform with law, nor even with the words of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury). The Income Tax Act provides, in
March 5, 1973

section 220, that the Minister of National Revenue shall administer and enforce this act. Section 150 provides that a return of the income for each taxation year in the case of a corporation, or for each taxation year for which taxes are payable in the case of an individual, shall be filed without notice or demand with the minister in the prescribed form, containing the prescribed information. Certain legal requirements follow from these provisions.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-INTENTION RESPECTING EXTENSION OF RUNWAYS AT MALTON
AIRPORTS-INTENTION RESPECTING EXTENSION OF RUNWAYS AT MALTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 30 last the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) made an announcement in connection with airports in the Toronto region. We have received a lot of gobbledygook from the government in connection with airports in the Toronto region and it was for that reason I tried to get from the minister a specific answer in connection with the extension of runway facilities at the Toronto international airport at Malton.
The minister's answer was to the effect that the government at that time was not prepared to give any answers. That is the reason I have raised this matter in the adjournment debate tonight. Early in January of this year the Swackhamer report in connection with the Pickering airport hearings which were held last fall was tabled in this House. The evidence in the Swackhamer report in connection with the Pickering airport is that facilities at Malton could easily be extended to look after the anticipated air traffic growth in the Toronto area until the year 2000. Shortly after that report was filed, the Minister of Transport was good enough to entertain some members from this side of the House with members from the ministry who were involved in the Pickering matter and, indeed, in air transport throughout that portion of Ontario served by the Toronto international airport, the Hamilton airport and other places.
At that time members of the minister's staff indicated to myself and to others that in their opinion the expansion of
Adjournment Debate
Malton was virtually an impossibility. In 1968 the whole question of expansion of Malton airport was brought to public meetings in the town of Mississagua, and at that time it was clearly demonstrated that if further north-south runways were created, at least 100,000 people would be severely affected. At that time the decision seemed to have been made by the minister that there would be no expansion at Malton.
Further, we hear after the notice in respect of the Pickering site that the minister now intends to conduct an inquiry, not an inquiry after the expropriation but none the less an inquiry as to the need for an airport at Pickering and, indeed, an inquiry into the whole airport need at Toronto. So the people who live in the town of Mississagua are confused in not knowing, on the one hand, the extent to which Malton can be expanded and whether Pickering is absolutely necessary and no expansion can take place at all. On the other hand, they know that there is to be an inquiry to see whether Pickering is necessary.
The whole situation leaves everyone in a flux. People who own houses do not know, people who have businesses do not know, people who are taxpayers do not know, and the municipality which is required to service the area does not know. The simple question is a question of the runway. Can this ministry or the government assure this town that a runway or further runways, particularly north-south runways at the Malton site are needed, or whether they will be installed? The ministry has told me and others that a further runway built, say, 1,000 feet west of the existing north-south runway would be only 20 per cent effective. The ministry has said that runways need to be at least 5,000 feet apart. If this is so, and if there is no more land for such a runway, it should be no problem for the minister to flatly declare it is not the intention of the government to increase runway facilities at the Malton airport. But the answer given is that it is not the intention of the government to do so. This is the reason for this debate. This is the reason why I again ask the government to come clean and to say what it intends to do with respect to Malton.

YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANT DISTRIBUTION AMONG INCOME CLASSES-CONSULTATION ON WEEKLY PAY RATE WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to pursue a question which I raised in the House back in January on the Opportunities for Youth program. I had hoped that this issue might be debated earlier than this since the deadline for Opportunities for Youth applications was March 1. Nevertheless, I would like to pursue the point on the questions I raised because I do not believe the minister gave a full and adequate reply. The concern that I raised earlier was: What guarantee is there

March 5, 1973
Adjournment Debate
that an equitable proportion of OFY grants go to the youth of various income classes, especially to young people of low income families?
The problem, as I see it, is that we have a government designed and implemented program which is called Opportunities for Youth, but in reality it has become a program of opportunities for students and mostly students in the middle and upper income groups. If we look at some figures for 1971-I am sorry that I do not have the more recent, 1972 figures, if indeed they have been tabulated-we see that the percentage of young people unemployed ran at 15 per cent for post-secondary students and at 20 per cent for non-students.
In the same year we find that 62 per cent of the applicants for Opportunities for Youth grants were postsecondary students and only 26 per cent were non-student applicants. Of the post-secondary applicants, 68 per cent were successful in their applications, but of the non-students only 17 per cent were successful in receiving grants. Therefore we see that students have a greater acceptance rate than non-students. This is readily understandable. The students are more articulate; they can formulate their briefs much better than the non-students and hence enhance their chances of being selected.
We have a problem of goals. A program that began as Opportunities for Youth, in practice has become opportunities for students. I want to know, is this official government thinking? We have hints that it may be. In the 1971 task force report at page 29 we read:
The first objective of the program was to provide employment for students ... the priorities among this target group were postsecondary school students-
If this is what Opportunities for Youth has become, let the government admit it openly, but then let it be fair enough to design another program for the non-student young people, thousands of whom are unemployed, frustrated and angry. The second question I raised earlier asked, did the government consult the provincial ministries of education to determine whether the funds needed for the average student to see him through the year in university were comparable to what OFY was providing? The answer of the minister was no. This soon becomes evident. We see that the average earnings of post-secondary OFY participants in 1972 was $1,000 or $1,200 with an average saving of somewhere between $400 and $600. Mr. Speaker, such earnings cannot possibly cover tuition and living costs for today's university students. The government has set a maximum earning of $90 a week for OFY applicants, so even the OFY-or should I say the opportunities for students program-is not meeting the needs of the students.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to know, first, if the Opportunities for Youth program is now providing primarily opportunities for students. If it is not, what guarantees for equitable distribution of grants to youth of all income and occupational groups is there in the program? I want to know, secondly, if the minister will raise the pay allotted for the applicant so that what he earns can realistically meet the cost of a university education today. Likewise for the non-student, will the government

consider giving him an adequate wage so that he can live decently in today's society?

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary ol State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: YOUTH-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON GRANT DISTRIBUTION AMONG INCOME CLASSES-CONSULTATION ON WEEKLY PAY RATE WITH PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the first question as to whether the Opportunities for Youth program has been successful among under-privileged youth with low incomes, I might say that the Opportunities for Youth program has been very successful over the last two years. The funds that were granted to under-privileged youth show the government's concern for this particular group of people. The Opportunities for Youth Program came to grips with the problem of regional, ethnic, economic and social disparities, by granting the major part of the available funds to the young people who were having a hard time finding a summer job and who urgently needed financial assistance.
In 1972, most of the participants, that is 57 per cent, came from rural areas, which somewhat offsets the nonavailability of summer employment in those areas. The male representation that was dominant on projects in 1971 was reduced in 1972, and we managed to establish a ratio of 55 to 44 per cent. Although 65 per cent of Canadian students at the post-secondary level came from families with a gross income under $11,000, over 70 per cent of the participants at the post-secondary level came from families in that income bracket. Over 50 per cent of the students at the secondary level participating in the Opportunities for Youth program came from families with a gross income under $8,000.
As regards the second question, in respect of salaries, we admit that there were no formal consultations between the federal government and the provincial government. However, I should like to remind my honourable friend that the Opportunities for Youth program is not meant to settle all the employment problems of young people. However, the amount of $90 is a sizeable amount, nevertheless, and we think it was preferable, with a $40 million budget, $6 million more than last year, to try to reach a larger number of young people by paying them a weekly salary that is not the perfect solution but which can partly meet their needs.
And my honourable friend should not forget that only 15 per cent of the summer jobs were filled under the Opportunities for Youth program. Most of them, that is 85 per cent, happened to be filled by the private sector.
In closing, I would say to my hon. friend that young people must not consider the Opportunity for Youth program simply in terms of income but avail themselves of the opportunity to fulfil their personal ideas, to get involved positively in social achievement and to get ready for the tasks of tomorrow.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAINS-MEASURES TO STOP PRICE INCREASE
AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAINS-MEASURES TO STOP PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 31 last, I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) concerning the excessive price increases of feed grains and proteins in eastern Canada.
March 5, 1973

My question was the following:
Can the minister tell us, after having met with the representatives of the Canadian Feed Manufacturers Association and the persons directly concerned with the matter in eastern Canada, what he intends to do to improve conditions concerning the price of feed grains?
The minister answered as follows:
-as I said before, the main cost is the high cost of proteins. There is a world shortage. I think the latest figures given to me show an increase of 140 per cent to farmers for these protein supplements. We will be making a decision next week as to how we will aid farmers caught in this cost-price squeeze.
Mr. Speaker, the present situation of farmers in eastern Canada, and particularly in the riding of Richmond which I represent, is very difficult. Many factors have caused this price increase in feed grains in the last few years, an increase which I consider as very difficult for producers, particularly milk producers. Canadian farmers have suffered a lot from the administration of the Liberal majority government between 1968 and 1972. Farmers, perhaps more than any other class of Canadians, have suffered during those four long years from the incoherence of the federal government in the field of agriculture.
During the years 1969-1970, the government paid the farmers of western Canada not to produce. They paid western grain producers to keep a large part of their prairies unploughed because according to them there were enormous surpluses of grains in the west and exports were in difficulty while the price of milk remained stationary.
Mr. Speaker, farmers from eastern Canada then had pay more for feed grain than what the Canadian government was getting for it in other countries.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture told me that such a situation was due to a world shortage of proteins. I can understand that if other countries, just as Canada, have paid grain producers not to produce which, as I said a while ago, has caused scarcity of grain on markets and has contributed to raise its price spectacularly. At home, for instance, in supermarkets around Sherbrooke and the Richmond constituency oats was selling at $2.23 per 100 lbs. in January 1971 and $4.10 in January 1973.
What did the Liberal government do to help farmers face this increase of close to 100 per cent?
The price of barley, of wheat, in short of all feed grains has more than doubled.
Soya, for instance, was the most affected. It was selling at $127 a ton in April 1972 whereas today it is selling at $260 per ton. And executives of the farmers co-operative in Sherbrooke told me today that they were expecting it to reach $300 a ton in June.
The UPA says that raising a hog in eastern Canada costs $4.36 more than in western Canada. I believe new measures involving feed grains should strive for parity between prices in the east and in the west of Canada. The UPA submitted to us a brief suggesting among other things that the Wheat Board should be the marketing body for feed grains on the domestic market outside the
Adjournment Debate
designated zone, that the grants for feed grains transportation should be an integral part of the marketing system of feed grains in Canada, that the initial prices-state-guaranteed maximum prices-for wheat, barley and oats should reflect production costs, that any policy aimed at improving grain prices in a reasonable way in the Prairie provinces should be accepted by Quebec provided milk producers always get equal treatment, that the right to deliver feed grains import licenses should be taken from the Wheat Board and given to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
In the last Speech from the Throne, the government committed itself to introducing a bill to establish price parity for feed grains throughout Canada. So, in my opinion, the government is aware of this problem and particularly of the fact that it was mistaken during the years 1969-70-71. Mr. Speaker, we are impatiently awaiting this new bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-FEED GRAINS-MEASURES TO STOP PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 13 last the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nolan) proposed a debate on the same question.
I answered that, in my opinion, his question was essentially the same as the one asked by the hon. member sitting to my right. I also said that my answer would be the same in both cases.
Instead of referring the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) to my previous answer, I am going to repeat it to him.
It can be found at page 6 of Hansard of January 4, in connection with the government's undertaking in the Speech from the Throne. I quote:
The Government supports the principle of an equitable relationship of prices of feed grain to livestock feeders in various areas of Canada.
Before the next crop year, the government intends to take steps to ensure maximum progress in the production of feed grains and stock breeding in Canada; I am convinced it will respect that commitment. We are now having important discussions with various groups of producers, to make sure they will be heard and their opinions will be taken into consideration in finding a solution. I know hon. members would not want decisions to be taken without consultation.
Mr. Speaker, the increase in farm production costs worries me and the fact that this increase stems from a world shortage of feed grains and proteins is of little comfort.
However, I am happy that this time, at least, the price feed grain consumers are getting for their production has also gone up. Let us hope that the rise in stock breeding production costs will also be reflected in better prices for the producer of feed grains and proteins, which will help him to stabilize his income while ensuring that he can produce even more feed grains next year.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will say that everyone is aware of the seriousness of the situation, and I know a practical solution will soon be found.

Statement by the
Secretary of State for External Affairs,
The Honourable Mitchell Sharp, to the Opening Session of the International Conference on Viet Nam,
Paris, February 26, 1973
Mr. Chairman,
The first words of any representative of Canada to an international conference on the subject of Viet Nam must be to congratulate the authors of the Agreement signed in this same building a month ago. All the parties deserve the gratitude not only of their own peoples but of all those states which have come to regard the war in Viet Nam as affecting their own national aspirations and interests. My government is firmly of the opinion that the Agreement signed here last month represents a magnificent and hard-earned opportunity which must not be lost. This agreement, indeed, doesn't solve all the problems, neither does it meet all of our hopes; but it's very existence is far more desirable than the absurdity of the armed conflict itself.
Although Canada's agreement to participate in the International Commission of Control and Supervision was conditional, the Canadian Delegation in Saigon has taken a leading part in getting not only the International Commission of Control and Supervision teams in place as required by the agreement, but also in facilitating the other organizations established under it to begin to exercise their functions. The Canadian Delegation from the beginning has been motivated by a desire to make the agreement work if this was at all possible. This will continue to be our attitude in Viet Nam for as long as we are there. It will also be the attitude of the Canadian Delaga-tion here in Paris. I am sure that all other delegations at this conference are equally conscious of the importance of the part this conference has to play in transforming the present precarious ceasefire into a lasting peace in which the South Vietnamese people and only the South Vietnamese people will determine their future. Even though the Lao and Khmer peoples are not represented at this
conference, their futures too are bound up in peace in Viet Nam. They too are entitled to the right to determine their own futures for themselves without any foreign intervention.
The fact that there is yet another international conference being held on Viet Nam is in some respects sad inasmuch as it reflects on the rights of the Indochinese peoples to determine their own futures for themselves. But the fact remains that the struggle in Indochina has become an international struggle involving not only the nations of that peninsula but countries far removed from it. From the point of view of my government, the object of the Paris Agreement is not to perpetuate an international presence in Viet Nam but to eliminate it and on conditions that will ensure again a fresh internationalization. This conference should be able to provide for some of those conditions.
Canada has had the educative experience of having served 19 years on the international commissions in Indochina and from that experience we have come to a number of conclusions. If these conclusions seem to imply criticism of the existing agreement of Viet Nam, I hasten to assure you that this is not my intention. My primary purpose is to prevent my country from being once more involved in an intractable situation and an open-ended commitment. At the same time we are deeply conscious that Canada has a history of concern for and participation in international peacekeeping and is very jealous of its reputation in this area.
Canada sees itself, in its membership in the International Commission of Control and Supervision, not as the spokesman of any one point Of view and certainly not as serving any direct national policy of its own, but as a representative of the International Community and invited by all the parties concerned to act as such. We therefore feel that we have an obligation not only to the parties to the agreement and indeed to this conference if it should decide to maintain an active interest in this agreement, but to the International Community as a whole.
We would obviously prefer to see all peace supervisory operations conducted under the auspices of the United Nations in accordance with the charter. The fact that this has not been possible in the case of Indo-China reinforces, in our view, the obligation of the International Commission of Control and Supervision to act as if it were representing the world community. If this were not so it would be merely a quadripartite group with no claim to the description international in its title. Canada would have preferred greater Asian participation not only in the International Commission but also in this International Conference which is to discuss matters of vital concern to the future peace and stability of the Asian region. It is in the attempt to engage the International Community to the greatest extent possible that we have adopted the policy of giving full information on our International Commission of Control and Supervision participation. Apart from details of negotiations while they are still under way, we feel that the International Community has a right to know what is being done in its name in Viet Nam. For our part we propose to report regularly and publicly on this at least until other more satisfactory means are found for
25789-49£

March 5, 1973
transmitting information and points of view to all concerned in the International Community.
As I have already mentioned, our primary concern is to do what we can to make Canadian participation in the International Commission of Control and Supervision effective. We wish to continue to serve and we ask this conference to make it possible for us to do so. In this connection we have come here to seek your support in establishing an independent mechanism more representative of the International Community than the existing mechanism, through which the International Commission of Control and Supervision or any of its members could report and which would provide for some possibility of appropriate reaction to such reports.
But we also have another concern. I have no authority to speak for other member countries of the International Commission of Control and Supervision but my government, as the government of a responsible country, could not accept the onus of passing to the former belligerents in Indo-China reports that could conceivably result in a re-escalation of the war in Indo-China. At the same time, we are not prepared to suppress information once we are satisfied that it is soundly based. For this reason Canada has consistently stated a fundamental condition to its participation: that it would serve on the International Commission in Viet Nam only if among other things this conference produced some more broadly-based international authority which would accept the responsibility for evaluating and, if necessary, acting upon reports from the International Commission, or its members, dealing with the manner in which the agreement was being carried out. Ideally, as I have said before, the Security Council of the United Nations should be the body responsible for receiving reports from the International Commission of Control and Supervision or its members and determining what, if any, action is required. Reluctantly, we are prepared to acknowledge that this solution is not practicable in the present situation but we must have some acceptable substitute. In any event, Canada considers that the Secretary General of the United Nations who has been invited to this conference by the United States and the Democratic Republic of Viet Nam on behalf of the parties to the agreement would provide the most appropriate and effective channel for receiving and transmitting the views of the International Commission. He is present here not only as the principal public servant of the world, but as representative of the world's concern at the decades of warfare in Viet Nam. His obviously disinterested position fits him uniquely for this task. I should make it clear that I do not propose that the Secretary-General assume any responsibility either in this capacity or on behalf of the United Nations for action consequent upon his transmission of information received from the International Commission during the interim period of its involvement in Viet Nam. If however it is agreed that the membership of this conference constitutes the continuing political authority to which the International Commission of Control and Supervision should report, the Secretary-General should in our view also be vested with the task of reconvening the conference when requested to do so on whatever basis we may here decide. I would like to circulate and table a
resolution which could cover the kind of arrangement I have in mind.
My government is well aware of the problems that a vacancy in the International Commission of Control and Supervision could create and would, in practice, do whatever it could to avoid that situation arising. But we should not be asked to watch in silence a resumption of hostilities nor to accept direct responsibility for all the consequences that could ensue if we felt duty-bound to report to the world that the agreement has been seriously breached.
We will work to find a solution that would meet our reasonable requirements. We are willing to examine any proposal that offers any chance of meeting our point. This is one of the reasons why, at the very beginning of the conference, I am putting forward a resolution that would best meet our requirements and we hope it will be given the most serious consideration. Although this is only one of a number of factors in our decision-making, we shall examine the results of this conference with the greatest care and in the light of the information we have received from our delegation in Viet Nam. Should we decide as a result of our study of the outcome of this conference and of our experience up to now, that we must terminate our membership on the International Commission of Control and Supervision, we would so inform all the interested parties that at the end of the 60 days for which we undertook to serve, that is, on March 30, Canada would cease to be a member of the International Commission of Control and Supervision. At the same time, however, we would declare our willingness, if all the parties signatory to the agreement so desired, to reamin in place and act as a member until April 30, 1973, or such earlier date as a new member could be agreed upon by the signatories and take our place.
Such a decision would be a very sad one for my government to have to make. All Canadians have taken justifiable pride in the manner in which the armed forces of Canada in particular have contributed to peacekeeping operations through out the world. It would be a bitter disappointment to them and to us to have to terminate our participation unilaterally. But I am satisfied that no Canadian would wish to see our representatives placed in the position of having to choose between suppressing relevant information or accepting full and direct national responsibility for the possible consequences of transmitting it under the existing arrangements. Even less would the Canadian people wish to see our delegation stand idly by, as Canadian delegations in Indo-China have had to do in the past, while agreements they are supposed to supervise are disregarded.
I am hopeful that the new agreement will succeed if there is a desire on the part of those present to help make it succeed and to involve themselves in the process. If I am wrong we shall have to arrange for the orderly transfer of our International Commission of Control and Supervision responsibilities to some other government. In doing so we would not be suggesting that our partners in the International Commission or a potential successor would be less sensitive or less alert to the problems that could arise than we were. We reached our own conclusions on peace-keeping in Viet Nam some years ago and
March 5, 1973

we have no reason to doubt their validity. On the other hand, we can readily understand that other countries differently situated from Canada could come to quite different conclusions. We respect their points of view and hope that they will understand ours.
Canada was invited to this conference as a member of the International Commission of Control and Supervision and its participation now and in any final act or declaration is linked to our continued participation in the International Commission of Control and Supervision. It follows, therefore, that a cessation of Canadian participation in the International Commission of Control and Supervision would also mean a termination of any other Canadian responsibilities that might arise out of either the agreement and protocols or any acts or declarations emanating from this conference.
I have asked the head of our delegation in Saigon, who happens like myself, to be chairman at the present time, to give me an interim report on the work of the International Commission of Control and Supervision and the state of affairs in respect to the implementation of the agreement and protocols.
The report that I received late last week from the head of the Canadian delegation made two points very clearly: first, the ceasefire has not been effective throughout South Viet Nam, and, second, the four-party joint military commission has not operated effectively. Both these factors have seriously impaired the Commission's ability to meet its obligations.
With respect to the ceasefire, it is evident from this report that the Vietnamese parties are still engaged in hostile activities related to efforts by one side or the other to enlarge its areas of control. The Commission has received numerous complaints from the four parties alleging violations of the ceasefire. In a number of cases investigations have been ordered but, at this early stage, we have been obliged to settle for investigations of a more limited scope than that envisaged in the agreement, debate within the commission over what the commission is empowered to investigate and at whose request, delays on the part of the four-party joint military commission in establishing itself in the field, and the conditions of insecurity prevailing in the countryside as a result of continued hostilities-all these have militated against the commission's ability to take decisive action in investigating most ceasefire violations. After receiving a series of general complaints alleging ceasefire violations, the commission issued a strong appeal to the parties to respect the ceasefire. This appeal on February 16 predated by one day an appeal by the four-party joint military commission to the same effect.
The delay in the four-party joint military commission in becoming fully effective has presented the International Commission with serious problems in meeting its obligations with respect to the deployment of teams in the field. The Commission's regional headquarters teams were deployed on February 5, several days after the deadline imposed upon us. On February 20, the commission decided to deploy its teams at the subregional level. In addition, the commission has decided to deploy its teams to points of entry into South Viet Nam to control the import of
armaments and other military material, as well as four teams to observe the withdrawal of United States forces and other forces allied with the Republic of Viet Nam, from South Viet Nam. Every effort is being made by the Canadian delegation to ensure that teams in the regions and at points of entry are deployed within the deadline established by the agreement, that is to say, by February 27. Whether we succeed in meeting this deadline will depend, as everything will depend on the ability of the four parties to afford the necessary co-operation. We have however taken the position that the inability of the four party joint military commission to function smoothly should not necessarily be permitted to bring a halt to the attempts of the International Commission to meet its obligations.
We have been pleased to note the progress of the exchange of prisoners-of-war and foreign civilian personnel. This has been an operation in which the four parties, despite some initial difficulties, have exhibited an ability to cooperate and coordinate their activities. We can only hope that the cooperative spirit that has characterized this operation will be extended to the implementation of all other provisions of the agreement.
Simultaneously with its attempts to deal with substantive issues and to deploy its field machinery, the commission has been engaged in setting up its headquarters in Saigon, establishing its procedures, securing support facilities, and organizing a secretariat. This has been a complex and lengthy process which has not yet been completed, despite concentrated effort. Among the difficulties the commission has encountered in this area of its work is the fact that neither the agreement nor its protocols made provision for a secretariat, even though the necessity of establishing one was obvious. Personnel additional to the ceilings established in the protocol will be required if delegates are to be in a position to staff the secretariat adequately.
Fellow delegates, this, then, is the Canadian view of the status of the International Commission of Control and Supervision as of the last day or so. There are continuing problems of implementation and there remains the matter of a reporting authority for the Commission and its members. Implementation is the responsibility of the parties to the agreement assisted as best it can by the International Commission of Control and Supervision. However, the matter of providing an adequate international political authority as a basis for the operation and reporting of the International Commission of Control and Supervision and its members is clearly the main responsibility of this conference. My delegation will spare no effort in helping to achieve this objective on which we think so much depends. Thank you.

March 5, 1973
Statement by the
Secretary of state for External Affairs of Canada,
The Honourable Mitchell Sharp, to The International Conference in Paris,
Plenary Session, March 1,1973 Canada supports the spirit of the act of this Conference. We also wish to associate ourselves with the expressions of goodwill and co-operation reflected throughout this conference and underlined in the document before us. For these reasons, we are prepared to sign it. I wish to make it clear, however, that we will have to assess the provisions of Articles 6 and 7 in particular, as to whether they are sufficient to meet one of the major requirements we have consistently stated as being essential to the ultimate effectiveness of the International Commission of Control and Supervision, on the basis of our quarter century experience in international supervision in Viet Nam and elsw-here throughout the world. In very general terms Articles 6 and 7 represent one approach; an effort has undoubtedly been made to meet our requirement but does it go far enough and will it work? Our concept of an independent continuing political authority is contained in the proposal tabled by me in my statement of February 26. The
arrangements provided in Articles 6 and 7 will be reviewed carefully by the Canadian Government as it carries out its consideration of the extent to which the various conditions we have stated to be essential to our continued participation in the commission beyond the initial period of sixty days have been, or, are likely to be fulfilled.
I must add that in signing the act of this conference, I am not accepting any responsibilities on behalf of Canada that are not determined by our initial participation in the commission, nor by previously announced Canadian policy. Finally, Canada considers itself bound by the arrangements provided for in the Act only so long as it remains on the Commission and should Canada find it necessary to terminate its participation in the International Commission of Control and Supervision, it would no longer consider itself formally bound by the terms of the act of the conference. I can, nevertheless, assure this distinguished company that Canadians would, as a matter of policy and as a matter of principle, remain committed to the promotion of the achievement by the peoples of Indochina of a stable and peaceful situation, and our acts would reflect this commitment.
Tuesday. March 6. 1973
